Voters have spoken. What does it mean for renters, homebuyers, sellers, and the housing industry? I'm Danielle Hale, Chief Economist at Realtor.com, and this is The Weekly Housing Outlook your guide to the best research and insights on the economy and housing market. Featured Report Before we get into the election impact, today’s feature is the October 2026 Luxury Housing Report in which Senior Economist Anthony Smith outlines what we’re seeing at the high-end of the housing market. The key takeaway from this analysis is that luxury prices continue to soften, with the entry-level luxury price dipping 2.3% from a year ago in October. This is the 31st consecutive month of year-over-year easing in the national entry-level luxury price point which now stands at $1.2 million. Among more exclusive luxury tiers, we saw somewhat larger price declines with the high-end luxury price dipping more than 4 percent and the ultra-luxury price falling more than 6 percent. As top prices soften, we’re seeing somewhat fewer million-dollar listings on the market. One area of stability is among the country’s most expensive markets, which continue to be found in coastal areas such as Bridgeport CT, Los Angeles CA, and Naples FL where luxury prices are 2 to 3 times the typical U.S. entry-luxury price. Because most of the priciest markets are seeing prices soften, Anthony decided to explore those luxury markets where home prices are moving in the opposite direction. Among our study set, 12 posted luxury price growth of 1 percent or more. In general, these fastest growth markets are not necessarily the priciest. Two-thirds of them have a luxury-entry price below $2 million. However, Naples, Florida stand out. It topped the list as the market with the fastest price growth of 9 percent which is quite a feat considering it also has the third highest entry-luxury price in the nation. The Week Ahead: Now, to the week ahead. We have a packed week of insights from Realtor.com Economics. On Monday, Senior Economist Anthony Smith published the October Luxury Report, which we’ve just discussed. On Tuesday, we honor America’s military service members and veterans with a report on VA loans just in time for Veteran’s Day. Senior Economist Jiayi Xu explores what VA loans are and how they help with homeownership. On Wednesday, Senior Economist Hannah Jones examines how the lock-in effect has evolved and where today’s homeowners with a mortgage face larger or smaller payment shocks if they are thinking about moving. On Thursday, Hannah is back to examine what the first full week of November data reveals about the housing market, and on Friday, Hannah publishes the October Hottest Markets report, which identifies the markets where homes are moving fastest and getting the most attention from online shoppers. Turning to the macro indicators that will be released, we’ll see the consumer price index reading on inflation as well as mortgage rates and existing home sales. Inflation has run above the Fed’s target, 2% growth in headline PCE, for 5 and a half years, and it’s clear from exit polls that the cost-of-living was very much on the mind of voters in last week’s election. This week we’ll see the first inflation reading for October from the consumer price index which was up sharply in September largely due to higher energy prices. I’m expecting the annual inflation reading to be similarly high in October even if the month-to-month momentum wanes a bit. Although inflation remains elevated, mortgage rates could continue to ebb. Last week the 30-year fixed mortgage rate according to Freddie Mac dropped to 7.18 percent as the 10-year hovered near 4.9 percent. Late in the week, the 10-year yield dropped further as uncertainty over AI investments led to a sharp pullback in stocks. Even if the 10-year were to bounce back to 4.9%, it has adjusted faster than mortgage rates, so I think there is room for spread compression that could help nudge rates lower, which will help late-season home shoppers. The last indicator of the week is existing-home sales data from the National Association of Realtors. October home sales data is likely to be very disappointing. The 95th percentile threshold fell 4.1% and the 99th percentile fell 6.2%. Luxury homes are selling faster: The median luxury listing spent 73 days on the market, 5 days faster than last year, while the median listing overall took 63 days, essentially flat. Million-dollar listings slipped to 12.3% of the market, down 0.5 percentage points. Bridgeport tops the most expensive markets: Bridgeport-Stamford-Danbury, CT took the #1 spot, with the 10% most expensive listings starting at $3,960,000 (3.3 times the national luxury entry price). Naples was the only top 10 market with a year-over-year gain (up 9.0%). items.title: Mortgage Rates Dip Ahead of a Big Week for Inflation Data
items.description: Mortgage Rates Dip Ahead of a Big Week for Inflation Data Published on November 9th, 2026 by Chen Zhao In A Nutshell: Mortgage rates are coming down as investors dial back expectations for rate hikes. But that could change: Key inflation data comes out this week. Last Week’s Highlights Two highlights from a busy election week: The landslide win for Democrats could impact markets in two ways. One, markets are starting to price in some political risk to the AI boom because Democratic officials are expected to limit the buildout of data centers. Two, there’s now a higher likelihood of stalemates during budget negotiations and debt limit increases. Friday’s jobs report barely made a splash, even though it was significantly stronger than expected. The economy is now adding about 100,000 jobs per month, likely a bit above the breakeven rate given the low rate of immigration. The unemployment rate remains at historical lows and wages are still increasing 3.1% annually. Upcoming Attractions This week’s economics highlight is the CPI inflation data coming Tuesday, coupled with Friday’s PPI data. Together, the two will form a complete picture of the core PCE inflation measure the Fed uses. The consensus forecast has core CPI coming in at 0.2% month-over-month, down slightly from last month. Forecasters are expecting a small statistical distortion in the data due to last year’s government shutdown. A very low read for inflation might convince the Fed to hold off on hiking rates at the December meeting, but they could just as easily write it off as one data point. They would evaluate how broader financial conditions have changed since the last meeting, including any further improvement in rates. Many Fed officials are holding speaking engagements this week. The ones to watch are Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan on Tuesday; Vice Chair Michelle Bowman on Monday, Tuesday, and Friday; Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack on Thursday; and New York Fed President John Williams on Thursday. items.description: Cushman & Wakefield Brokers $44 Million Sale of 240-Unit Apartment Community in Sheboygan, Wisconsin to Axiom Properties Jeremy Barewin • 11/9/2026 The Corridor garnered significant investor interest, attracting more than 25 offers The Corridor SHEBOYGAN, WISC. -- Cushman & Wakefield (NYSE: CWK), a leading global real estate services firm, today announced that its Multifamily Advisory Group has brokered the $44 million sale of The Corridor, a 240-unit Class A multifamily community in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, to Axiom Properties. Cushman & Wakefield's Brad Smith, Jack Maloney and Ralph Depasquale represented the seller, Chicago-based Midloch Investment Partners. Located at 1436 Green Street, the community was approximately 97% occupied at the time of sale. Under the seller's ownership, occupancy increased by nearly 25 percentage points in roughly 13 months. The sale also includes an in-place tax increment financing (TIF) agreement, which reimburses 65% of the incremental property tax through 2038 and enhances cash flow for the new owner. The Corridor benefits from a location within 30 minutes of more than 60,000 jobs, including major regional employers such as Kohler, Aurora Health Care, Sargento and Rockline Industries. Within a five-mile radius of the property, apartment occupancy exceeds 97%, while the area has seen no new multifamily deliveries since 2024 despite a sizeable population of renter households earning $50,000 or more annually. "Tertiary Midwest markets supported by strong employment fundamentals and limited new supply are attracting significant investor interest," said Smith, Managing Director, Cushman & Wakefield. "We received 25 offers from institutional, national, regional and private buyers, underscoring the depth of demand for stable, insulated markets like Sheboygan. As one of the largest multifamily transactions in the market in recent years, The Corridor presented a rare opportunity to acquire a high-quality asset with both strong in-place performance, cash flow stability and future upside." Completed in 2021 on a 13.44-acre site, The Corridor features one-, two- and three-bedroom residences across three residential buildings, along with a fitness center, resident lounge, community room, dog park, playground, outdoor gathering spaces and parking. Apartment homes feature granite countertops, stainless steel appliances, luxury vinyl plank flooring, in-unit washers and dryers, and select private balconies. Residents also enjoy convenient access to downtown Sheboygan, Lake Michigan beaches, retail destinations and recreational amenities. In 2025, the firm reported revenue of $10.3 billion across its core service lines of Services, Leasing, Capital markets, and Valuation and other. items.title: Residential Building Worker Wage Growth Rebounds, but Real Wages Continue to Decline
items.description: Residential Building Worker Wage Growth Rebounds, but Real Wages Continue to Decline November 9, 2026 Jing Fu No Comments Wage growth for residential building workers showed signs of a modest rebound in September 2026 following a sharp slowdown earlier in the year. According to the latest data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics , nominal wage growth picked up from its June pace, although it remained relatively modest. After adjusting for inflation, real wages continued to decline, indicating persistent pressure on workers’ purchasing power. In nominal terms, average hourly earnings (AHE) for residential building workers increased 2.8% year-over-year in September 2026, reaching $40.69 per hour. This marked an acceleration from the 1.2% year-over-year increase recorded in June 2026. After accounting for inflation, real wages declined 0.9% year-over-year in September 2026 to $12.1 per hour. Real wage growth strengthened temporarily during parts of 2024, reaching a peak of 6.2%, but has since weakened as nominal wage gains moderated and inflation continued to erode purchasing power. Meanwhile, the number of open, and unfilled construction sector jobs increased in September. Continued strength in construction-related activity, including data center construction, is supporting demand for construction workers. Despite the recent moderation in wage growth, residential building workers continue to earn relatively competitive wages compared with workers in other industries: 9.8% higher than the manufacturing sector ($37.06 per hour) 24.5% higher than the transportation and warehousing sector ($32.68 per hour) 3.6% lower than the mining and logging sector ($42.23 per hour) Note: Data used in this post relates to all employees in the residential building industry. items.title: Servicers need to update analytics as retention rate drops
items.description: Servicers need to update analytics as retention rate drops By Colin McNamara Published November 09, 2026, 1:53 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Expert Quote: "Traditional rate-based retention strategies aren't effective for borrowers who are motivated by access to equity" — Bob Hart, President of Mortgage Technology at ICE Supporting Data: Cash-outs accounted for 75% of all refinance-portfolio attrition in the third quarter. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Servicers are losing business as retention rates drop, signaling a need for more advanced analytics and a better understanding of borrowers. Refinance retention dropped four percentage points to 27% from the second to third quarter, according to the Intercontinental Exchange's latest mortgage monitor report . The retention among rate-and-term refinancers fell nine percentage points to 30%, while cash-out retention held at 26%. Servicers retained just 15% of cash-out borrowers who took out loans in 2019 or earlier. Processing Content "Get more advanced with your analytics," Andy Walden, head of mortgage and housing market research at ICE, told National Mortgage News. "Get deeper insight in terms of who's refinancing and why they're refinancing, and really incorporate that cash-out refinance scoring and propensity to refinance into your marketing effort." Andy Walden, head of mortgage and housing market research at ICE (Intercontinental Exchange) Cash-outs accounted for 75% of all refinance-portfolio attrition, which is a harder group to retain. Equity was the clear focal point for borrowers looking to refinance, and servicers who ran an in-the-money analytic off their book missed a large chunk of potential business, Walden added. "Traditional rate-based retention strategies aren't effective for borrowers who are motivated by access to equity rather than interest rate savings," said Bob Hart, president of mortgage technology at ICE, in a press release Monday. "To retain these borrowers, servicers need better visibility into their equity positions and the ability to engage them before they look elsewhere." Home equity continues to grow Borrowers collectively held a record third-quarter high $17.5 trillion in home equity, up 1.4% year over year. Tappable equity that can be accessed while maintaining a 20% cushion rose 1.2% to an average of $204,000 per borrower, a $16,600 jump from a year ago, according to the report. The number of equity millionaires also hit a third quarter record, as 2.4 million mortgage holders had at least $1 million in equity, a 6% increase from the same period last year. California accounted for 49% of the country's equity millionaires, followed by New York at 8% and New Jersey at 6%, the report found. "Home equity products, lines of credit and second liens continue to be the focal point for the market that drove the bulk of equity extraction in the first half of this year," Walden said. "Understanding borrowers and where they stand, ... whether they're a cash-out refinance or a home equity line of credit candidate, and making sure you have those pipelines set up and flowing; that's the key part from an equity standpoint." In a high-rate environment , cash-outs made up a greater share of refinances, as homeowners gave up historically low mortgage rates and took on higher monthly payments to access equity. Cash-out transactions accounted for roughly 14% of rate locks in recent weeks, while purchase loans represented 80% of rate locks, according to the report. Adjustable-rate mortgages made up more than 10% of early October rate locks as Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed-rate mortgage surged above 7%. The points-adjusted spread between 5/1 ARMs and 30-year fixed loans expanded from about 75 basis points this summer to more than 100 basis points early last month, further increasing the attractiveness of ARMs. That spread has since narrowed to about 87 basis points, the report found. items.title: NAR sees pent-up demand waiting on lower mortgage rates, better sentiment
items.description: The U.S. housing market is building “significant” pent-up demand that could be released if mortgage rates ease, inventory improves and consumer confidence rebounds, National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) chief economist Lawrence Yun told attendees Friday at NAR’s NXT in New Orleans. Yun contrasted today’s sales environmen t with the year 2000, noting that the U.S. population has grown from 281 million to 350 million and payroll jobs from 132 million to 159 million over that period. Housing wealth has ballooned from $7 trillion to $35 trillion, yet existing-home sales are tracking near 4 million this year , well below the 5.2 million homes sold in 2000, he said, citing NAR data. “Affordability is tough, but people’s incomes are rising, and if somehow mortgage rates go down, think about the potential housing demand that could be released to the marketplace,” Yun said. On the supply side, Yun said inventory has risen as sales have slowed. Months’ supply is now at its highest level since 2015, and the median home took 33 days to go from listing to contract in September, according to NAR. “Homes are staying on the market a little longer than before,” Yun said. “With longer days on market, you have to be realistic to the market condition. Otherwise, buyers will reject the homes on the market.” Yun pointed to consumer psychology as a key missing ingredient. Consumer sentiment has fallen to roughly half its 2000 level and is now worse than during the Great Recession, even as the labor market has added jobs. “If we can boost confidence levels, maybe that can also change the dynamics,” Yun said. First-time buyers remain near historic lows Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research, presented findings from the trade group’s newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers . First-time buyers made up 22% of all buyers, near the series low, and the median age of first-time buyers held at a record-high 40. Those numbers underscore how younger households are delaying homeownership, even as they form households and enter peak earning years. For lenders and real estate brokerages, that means fewer entry-level transactions and more emphasis on move-up or equity-rich buyers. “ First-time home buyers are struggling,” Lautz said. “They’re not struggling just with housing affordability. They're also struggling with rent. They’re struggling with student loan debt, and a rising issue for first-time home buyers is childcare costs.” Lautz noted that sellers reported staying in their homes for a median of 12 years before selling, the longest tenure on record for the survey. “The golden handcuffs of low interest rate mortgages is true. People are holding on to those properties for longer periods of time,” she said. “It’s why we need to build more housing inventory—especially affordable housing inventory—for the potential first-time home buyers who are out there.” Agent usage hits record highs Despite technology and direct-to-consumer platforms, use of licensed professionals in transactions remained strong, according to NAR’s survey. A reported 90% of buyers purchased through an agent, the highest share in four decades, and a record 92% of sellers used an agent. “Sellers want agents to price that home competitively, find that qualified buyer, help with marketing, and make sure they get to the closing table in a time frame that they need to do so,” Lautz said. Why this matters for housing professionals For real estate agents and brokers, NAR’s data point to a market where transaction volume is constrained more by affordability, rates and sentiment than by underlying demand. A larger population, more jobs and higher housing wealth suggest that activity could accelerate quickly if mortgage rates retreat and confidence improves. For lenders, a 22% first-time buyer share and a median first-time buyer age of 40 highlight both near-term headwinds and an eventual backlog of delayed demand. Households that are renting longer and juggling student debt and childcare may respond strongly to any easing in rates, pricing or down payment constraints. For builders and developers, Lautz’s comments reinforce the policy and business case for adding affordable inventory . With existing owners locked in by sub-4% mortgages and staying put for a median 12 years, new construction remains one of the few levers to ease the entry-level shortage. Yun’s and Lautz’s remarks come as the industry also adjusts to p ost-settlement commission rule changes and elevated borrowing costs , making accurate pricing, counseling on affordability and clear communication with consumers more central to winning business in 2027 and beyond. Residents can choose from nine distinct three- and four-bedroom townhome floor plans ranging from 1,798 to 2,168 square feet. Every home includes an attached two-car garage. Rents range from $2,500 to $3,190 a month. Community amenities include a resident clubhouse with an open-air pavilion and a rsaltwater pool. Residents also have access to an on-site dog park, game lawn, and outdoor grilling and dining stations featuring a Big Green Egg smoker. Partners on the project include Kimley-Horn (civil engineer and landscape architect), NRP Group (general contractor), and Vinyet (townhome architect). HARMON Melissa is part of Crescent Communities’ expanding HARMON portfolio, supported through its second joint venturepartnership with an account managed by Heitman LLC. The venture will continue to make investments in high-quality, intentionally crafted communities in key growth markets including Arizona, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Texas. items.title: Trademark And Morgan To Build Luxury Apartments In Oak Lawn: The DFW Deal Sheet
items.description: Two major commercial real estate firms began work on a luxury multifamily project that will occupy a full city block near Uptown. Courtesy of Trademark Property Co. A rendering of the multifamily community being built at 3900 Lemmon Ave. in Dallas Trademark Property Co. and Morgan Group broke ground on their 362-unit community at 3900 Lemmon Ave. in Dallas’ Oak Lawn neighborhood. The first apartments are expected to be completed in fall 2028, with full delivery to follow during the second quarter of 2029. “The opportunity to develop a full city block in Oak Lawn, adjacent to Turtle Creek, is rare, and Trademark put in the time and care to build a plan this neighborhood could support,” Stephen Frazee, Morgan’s DFW city development partner, said in a statement. Trademark led the site’s rezoning process, working with the Oak Lawn Committee, neighborhood stakeholders and the city of Dallas. Morgan will serve as the project’s developer, general contractor and property manager. The project team also includes GFF as architect, SJL Design Group as interior designer and LandDesign as landscape architect. SALES Ascent Real Estate Advisors acquired the 10-story Hillcrest Tower in Dallas from Albany Road Real Estate Partners. The building’s sale price was not disclosed, but the Dallas Central Appraisal District lists the property as being worth $16.3M for tax purposes. Hillcrest Tower was built in 1982 and renovated in 2022. The 168K SF office building at 12720 Hillcrest Road was 97% leased at the time of the deal. Ascent plans to build upon prior upgrades by refreshing the common areas and continuing to invest in move-in-ready spec-suites. Newmark represented the seller in the transaction. Dallas-based Sunwest Real Estate Group will provide property management services, and CBRE’s Trey Smith, Julee Amparo and Alix Kirby will lead leasing. *** Courtesy of Newmark The Colonnade at 15301, 15303 and 15305 North Dallas Parkway in Addison Cross Ocean Partners and Lincoln Property Co. acquired The Colonnade, a 1M SF office campus on nearly 12.5 acres along the Dallas North Tollway in Addison. The three-tower asset was sold through a receivership process on behalf of Trigild and CWCapital. The joint venture is committing $100M to reposition the property as a premier commercial hub for the market. Initial property improvements are underway, with the first phase of upgrades expected to be delivered throughout 2027. Newmark’s Stephen Schwalb, Chris Murphy, Robert Hill, Gary Carr and Austin Sheahan represented the seller in the transaction. Lincoln will provide management for the project, and the firm’s Jake Young, Christian Munoz and Hudson Dozier will lease the property. *** Mac Haik Auto Group purchased around 25 acres near the corner of Frontier Parkway and the Dallas North Tollway in Celina for a new 100K SF Chevrolet dealership. Mac Haik purchased the land from the family trust of Tom Mosey. Davidson Bogel Real Estate’s Ryan Turner, David Davidson Jr. and Edward Bogel represented the seller in the transaction. Mac Haik was represented by Sam Clayton and Adam Sheriff of Brown & Griffin Real Estate. *** California-based investor David Reid Properties purchased the nearly 38K SF Greenview Tech Centre Building E at 830 Greenview Drive in Grand Prairie. Built in 1981, the building offers flex industrial and office space. Marcus & Millichap’s Brad Mills marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a Florida-based investor, and procured the buyer. *** Dallas-based Paceline Equity Partners LLC and its joint venture partner, Aravest, sold the 308-key Renaissance Dallas at Plano Legacy West Hotel to Host Hotels & Resorts Inc. as part of a $374M deal that included another hotel in Brooklyn. Paceline and Aravest acquired Renaissance Plano in June 2023 and executed a strategy that added more rooms, reconfigured food and beverage outlets, and drove growth in room revenue and net operating income. CBRE Hotels served as exclusive adviser, while King & Spalding served as legal counsel to Paceline on the transaction. Bradford Commercial Real Estate Services’ Brian Pafford and Jared Laake represented the landlord, 2701 Plano Parkway Ltd. Colliers’ Allyson Yost represented the tenant in the deal. JLL’s Dallas office assisted with the capital raise, while Wintrust Bank provided the construction loan. items.title: Grange MPC begins second phase of development
items.description: Grange MPC begins second phase of development by Emily Marek November 09, 2026 The second phase includes Ricestead, Grange’s 20-acre amenity center. (via Johnson Development) Johnson Development’s Grange master-planned community in Katy has entered its second phase, with construction and sitework underway on an additional 500 homesites and a 20-acre amenity center. The new lots range from 40 feet wide up to 85 feet wide. The larger lots, which are new to the MPC, are suited for alley-access garages. Builders in this second phrase — including Highland Homes , J. Patrick Homes, David Weekley Homes, Newmark Homes, Chesmar Homes, Perry Homes, Drees Custom Homes, Westin Homes and Partners in Building — will receive 483 lots before the end of the year. “This is an exciting new chapter and a natural progression in our development of Grange,” the community’s vice president and general manager, Jacob Rice, said in a press release. “The demand is there for larger homesites which will allow our residents to move into more spacious homes in the community as their family needs dictate.” Construction is also underway on Ricestead , Grange’s 20-acre amenity center. Plans for the project include a resort-style pool, lap pool, pickleball and basketball courts and the Harvest Hall clubhouse, which will feature a fitness center and a co-working area. Space is also reserved for future retail offerings and a village green. “We view Ricestead as a modern-day town square where businesses and residents become true partners,” Rice added. “We envision people meeting for coffee, shopping local merchants and attending a concert or farmers market at the village green. Ricestead will move Grange from being a neighborhood to becoming a hometown.” Grange is currently home to over 500 residents in hundreds of new homes. Pricing in the community starts in the $300,000s. items.title: Remodeling Activity Holds Flat in Second Quarter Amid Housing Slowdown
items.description: Remodeling Activity Holds Flat in Second Quarter Amid Housing Slowdown November 9, 2026 Eric Lynch No Comments The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) has released its State Projections of Remodeling (SPR) for the second quarter of 2026. As a reminder, the SPR provides on a quarterly basis a state-level estimation of the market share and total dollar value of remodeling spending. The SPR is a statistical model designed to use national quarterly improvement spending data and estimate remodeling market share by state using multiple indicators and NAHB’s annual state remodeling forecast. Q2 2026 Results During the second quarter of 2026, remodeling spending at the national level came in at $271.2 billion on a seasonally adjusted annualized rate (SAAR), falling 2.3% from the previous quarter. Remodeling spending has decreased in five out of the past six quarters and is at its lowest level in two years. Nevertheless, remodeling spending has been larger than single-family construction spending for five straight quarters and accounts for 45.0% of residential construction spending. California had the largest market share of remodeling spending at 7.9%, or $21.4 billion, followed closely by Texas (7.3%, or $19.7 billion). Florida is third at 5.5%, or $14.8 billion, with New York (4.0%, or $10.8 billion) and North Carolina (3.0%, or $8.2 billion) rounding out the top five. When looking at the top ten states by the change in remodeling spending in the second quarter of 2026 (on a four-quarter moving average basis or 4QMA), Michigan saw its volume increase by $217.1 million, followed by Alabama (up $158.3 million), West Viriginia (up $140.6 million), Virginia (up $115.0 million), and Alaska (up $113.0 million). Except for the Northeast, all regions were represented within the top ten by change in spending. All ten experienced a growth rate of at least 1.7% year-over-year with a large concentration in smaller states. Only two of the top ten states by market share had a positive growth rate for the quarter (North Carolina and Illinois). Additionally, there was a fairly even split between states that had a negative growth rate (26) and those that had a positive growth rate (24) for the quarter, resulting in 0.0% average across all states. This corroborates NAHB’s forecast for the industry which expects inflation-adjusted spending to be flat-to-down for 2026. items.title: For Every Condo Buyer in the U.S., There Are More Than Two Sellers. That Gives Condo Buyers Strong Negotiating Power.
items.description: For Every Condo Buyer in the U.S., There Are More Than Two Sellers. That Gives Condo Buyers Strong Negotiating Power. Published on November 9th, 2026 by Dian Zhang and Asad Khan There were 123% more condo sellers than buyers nationwide in September, the widest gap since 2013, giving buyers extraordinary negotiating power. The number of condo buyers fell to its lowest level in 13 years, while the number of sellers ticked up. San Antonio had the country’s widest seller surplus, with more than five times as many condo sellers as buyers. Houston ranked second, followed by Miami at 274%. Only three metros had more condo buyers than sellers, led by Nassau County, NY, Newark, NJ and Milwaukee, WI. Condo buyers today have more negotiating power than they’ve had in at least 13 years. There were an estimated 123% more condo sellers than buyers nationwide in September, the largest gap in records dating back to 2013. The gap widened from 95.5% a year earlier. Redfin estimates the number of buyers using proprietary data on the typical time between a buyer’s first home tour and the closing of a purchase, along with MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers is based on active listings in the MLS. The figures in this report are national estimates. See the full methodology and explore the interactive dashboard . Redfin defines a buyer’s market as one with more than 10% more sellers than buyers, and a seller’s market as one with more than 10% more buyers than sellers. A market is considered balanced when the difference between sellers and buyers is within 10%. Other housing-market statistics, including median sale price, are based on Redfin’s analysis of MLS data. A buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily mean condos are affordable for buyers. The Number of Condo Buyers Fell to a Record Low The condo market has undergone a dramatic reversal since the pandemic-era homebuying boom. In September 2021, there were 25.1% fewer sellers than buyers. Five years later, the number of buyers fell 54%, while the number of sellers rose 36%. The shift has left sellers competing for a much smaller pool of potential buyers. The number of condo buyers fell to an estimated 88,460 in September, down 2.5 % from August and the lowest level in at least 13 years. Meanwhile, condo sellers totaled 197,248, up 0.9 % from the prior month. Several factors are weighing more heavily on the condo market than on the single-family home market. Rising insurance premiums, HOA fees and special assessments are making condos increasingly expensive to own, particularly in Florida and Texas , where hurricane risks and other natural disasters have contributed to higher insurance costs. That’s a problem for first-time buyers, who often turn to condos as a more affordable entry point into the housing market but lack equity from a previous home sale. While the condo market is challenging for buyers, those who can afford housing costs will have more power in negotiations. “For renters who have saved for a down payment and are ready to build equity, these buyer-friendly conditions are an opportunity,” said Asad Khan , a senior economist at Redfin. “Buyers have more options and a better chance of finding a place they like. Although condo prices and HOA fees remain relatively high, buyers have more room to negotiate price cuts, and condos are still generally more affordable than single-family homes.” The single-family market saw a similar trend in September, with the number of buyers dropping to a record low since 2013. Sellers outnumbered buyers by 53.7%–a wide gap, but less than half as wide as what we’re seeing in the condo market. The huge surplus of condo sellers over buyers is contributing to the record-breaking buyer's market in the overall housing market, which encompasses condos, townhouses and single-family homes Falling Condo Prices Offer Buyers Opportunities The national median condo sale price fell 0.8% to about $339,000 in September, the first year-over-year decline in five months. House hunters should keep in mind that the costs of buying and owning a condo extend beyond its purchase price, and those ongoing expenses can put additional pressure on buyers’ budgets. Rising homeowners association (HOA) fees and insurance premiums can push up the total monthly cost of ownership. Buyers should also consider the possibility of special assessments to cover major repairs or improvements to a building’s common areas. But for buyers who can afford the upfront costs of a condo and plan to stay put for several years, today’s buyer’s market may offer an opportunity. “Find a motivated seller and there are a lot of them,” said Cecilia Cordova , a Redfin Premier agent in Miami, who lives in a condominium herself. Researching the buildings you’d like to live in is the key to finding a financially healthy community and avoiding surprise assessment bills later, she said. Condo buyers have more options than they did years ago. “We have enough inventory for the next three to four years,” said Cordova. For prospective sellers? Cordova suggests considering renting their condo out for the time being. “If you really need to sell, the strategy is to list it lower than anybody else in the same building. It’s not time for you to try to experiment with a higher price,” she said. Today’s home prices and mortgage rates have made it harder for first-time homebuyers to enter the market, reducing demand for condos, which have traditionally served as an entry point to homeownership. The weekly average mortgage rate is 7.18% as of November 5, and home prices remain near historic highs. Sellers are increasingly dropping their asking prices to attract buyers, Redfin data shows. About 37% of condos that sold in September had a price reduction, compared with 16% during the pandemic-era housing boom five years earlier. items.title: Invitation Homes, HBI team up to train vets in skilled trades
items.description: Invitation Homes and Home Builders Institute (HBI) have formed a partnership to expand training and job placement for transitioning armed services members, veterans and their families seeking careers in construction, property maintenance and other skilled trades, according to a company announcement. The collaboration is part of Invitation Homes’ Invitation to SkillUp initiative and will support HBI’s Military Services program with hands-on, instructor-led training, industry-recognized certifications and job placement services. Under the agreement, HBI and Invitation Homes plan to connect HBI-trained veterans, military spouses and family members with roles in the build-to-rent and single-family rental sectors, expand recruitment at HBI Military Services locations including Fort Stewart, Georgia, and Jacksonville, Florida, and use Invitation Homes’ Veteran Employee Resource Group for mentorship and career guidance. The partners also aim to highlight success stories of veterans and family members who move into skilled trades careers. “Veterans and their families have dedicated themselves to serving our country, and we are proud to support them as they transition into rewarding civilian careers,” Invitation Homes President and CEO Dallas Tanner said in the release. “Through our Invitation to SkillUp initiative, we are investing in talented individuals whose dedication and service strengthen our communities, while helping create meaningful opportunities in the skilled trades.” HBI President and CEO Ed Brady said the nonprofit has spent the past decade training, certifying and placing transitioning military members, veterans and their families in skilled trades roles. Nearly 90% of its military program graduates secure jobs, earning on average more than three times the federal minimum wage, according to the announcement. “We know this model works, and with this important investment from Invitation Homes, we can help more veterans enter the skilled trades every year because the people who served this country deserve a career as strong as their service,” Brady said. Invitation to SkillUp is the company’s national skilled trades development platform, which partners with trade schools and workforce organizations across the country to broaden access to skills education and promote trades careers. Invitation Homes joins other national backers of HBI’s military programs, including The Home Depot Foundation and DEWALT . A recent $1 million gift from Google , followed by the new investment from Invitation Homes, underscores rising industry interest in supporting veterans and their families in building long-term skilled trades careers. For homebuilders, the partnership represents one more channel to address chronic labor shortages in residential construction and property maintenance by tapping into a pipeline of trained veterans at a time when the industry continues to struggle with aging trades workers and elevated repair and maintenance demand. items.title: Nicolas Retsinas, former Clinton housing official, dies
items.description: Nicolas Retsinas, former Clinton housing official, dies By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published November 09, 2026, 1:44 p.m. EST | Updated November 09, 2026, 1:51 p.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: After leaving government service, Nic Retsinas was a leader in affordable housing Expert Quote: "It was an honor for me to work with Nic." — Scott Olson Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Nicolas Retsinas, a former Clinton administration housing official, passed away on Nov. 4 after an extended illness; he was 79 years old. Details of his passing come from golocalprov.com, a website for his hometown of Providence, Rhode Island, as well as an online obituary. Processing Content In 1987, Retsinas became head of the Rhode Island Housing and Mortgage Finance Corp., a position he occupied until 1993. Later, he would return to become its board chair from 2015 through 2020. A statement posted on LinkedIn by the organization now known as RIHousing noted Retsinas "helped our agency start a new chapter. His impact is still present today in our work as a leading housing resource for Rhode Islanders, and his legacy will live on in the organizations, communities, and people he affected." Pres. Bill Clinton named Retsinas to be his Federal Housing Commissioner in 1993; in 1996, under the Vacancy Act, Clinton appointed him interim director of the Office of Thrift Supervision. Retsinas held the FHA post until 1998, at which time he left government service to become director of the Joint Center for Housing Studies at Harvard University. In his post-government service life, he would take board positions at the Center for Responsible Lending, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., the Federal Housing Finance Board, Freddie Mac, and the Neighborhood Reinvestment Corp., among other organizations. In addition, Retsinas was the chair of the board of directors of Habitat for Humanity International. He was inducted into the National Housing Hall of Fame. "Nic Retsinas believed that everyone deserved access to affordable, decent housing in thriving communities, and spent his professional life working to make that a reality," said Mike Calhoun, president of CRL, said in a press release. "He championed policy initiatives to address critical housing and community development needs. He also was a generous friend and mentor to many in the housing community." Retsinas' reforms while serving as FHA commissioner paved the way for the agency's critical role in preserving homeownership during the 2008 housing crisis, a statement from Scott Olson, executive director of the Community Home Lenders of America, said. "His commitment to affordable housing was evident in his enthusiasm for the cause, his record of public service, and his leadership at the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies," Olson said. "It was an honor for me to work with Nic. He will be sorely missed." At the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, Retsinas and his wife Joan endowed the Nicolas P. and Joan B. Retsinas Faculty Directorship, to ensure it will always be led by an eminent housing practitioner or scholar, the Center said in a LinkedIn post. "We are deeply saddened to share that Nic Retsinas, who led our Center from 1998 to 2010, has passed away," the post said. "Nic was a tireless advocate for inclusive, equitable housing policy, and his vision continues to shape our work." According to an online obituary, Retsinas is survived by his wife Joan; his children Amy Romero (Andrew), Jennifer Retsinas and Gregory Retsinas (Julie); and his sister Paulette Retsinas, along with five grandchildren. items.title: Trump strikes a softer note on immigration; builders need proof
items.description: On Sunday, President Donald Trump indicated that he is open to negotiating an immigration deal with the incoming Democratic Congress. However, despite softening post-election rhetoric, the Trump administration appears to be sending mixed signals on immigration, clouding the outlook for any potential bipartisan agreement. The stakes of the nation’s highly contentious immigration debate remain high for homebuilders. After a surge in job site raids by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) this summer and fall, many homebuilders say their workers, including those in the country legally, were swept up in enforcement actions . Whether a bipartisan immigration deal materializes remains an open and pressing question for the numerous builders facing ongoing job site disruptions. Speaking to CBS News’ 60 Minutes on Sunday, President Trump suggested his administration’s immigration policies “might be too tough” and may have contributed to last week’s election outcome. “When you go into a hotel…and you have a woman that's worked there as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress – a lot of good things, great jobs – and all of a sudden, they're being taken out of the country. It's tough. It's a tough thing,” Trump said. Trump added that it may be “doable” to reach an agreement allowing undocumented workers who have lived in the U.S. for many years, construction workers among them, to legally remain in the country. “Get the killers out. Get the rapists out. Get all the rough ones out. Get the drug dealers out, but let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them,” Trump suggested. The administration’s mixed messaging It’s unclear whether Trump’s softer rhetoric will translate into a bipartisan immigration deal. However, his administration’s decision to promote Stephen Miller, a longtime immigration hardliner, to White House Chief of Staff suggests an agreement may be less likely than Trump implied in his CBS News interview. And in a post on Sunday, the Official White House Rapid Response account, in a post on X , denied that Trump will push for an amnesty deal with Democrats. However, Trump has at times shown a willingness to soften his stance on immigration, at least briefly. In June 2025, the Trump administration momentarily directed ICE to pause job site raids in sectors like agriculture, hospitality and restaurants after facing blowback from business leaders worried about staffing shortages. Within days, however, the administration reversed course. It later set a target of 3,000 ICE arrests per day, leading to a record number of immigration arrests in recent months. Trump has also helped kill a bipartisan deal before. In early 2024, ahead of the presidential election, he urged Republicans to vote against a Senate border package introduced by Sen. James Lankford (R-OK) that would have tightened asylum requirements, ended releases of migrants into U.S. communities while they await hearings, and let the president close the border when asylum claims surged. The bill ultimately failed. Some homebuilding organizations, like the National Association of Home Builders, now have their eyes on a different bipartisan measure, the Dignity Act , which would allow certain undocumented workers to remain in the U.S. without citizenship. Trump’s words signaled openness to such a proposal, but the administration’s actions since the election suggest otherwise. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, laid out in a post-midterms election post on X that the administration may be open to changing its approach to immigration, with less room for negotiation. “Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement – by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you,” Vance wrote. For homebuilders, immigration policy and its impact on the construction labor pool remains among the biggest policy questions heading into 2027. However, history suggests that a bipartisan deal may be a heavy lift, as Washington hasn’t passed comprehensive immigration reform since 1986, under President Reagan. Whether Washington breaks its four-decade drought on immigration reform, and whether enforcement eases on job sites, remains a key policy wild card to watch in 2027. items.title: Macerich In Default On Almost $400M In Mall Debt
items.description: Wikimedia Commons/Charlie Brewer Macerich has defaulted on $399M in mall loans across two properties, the company announced in its third-quarter earnings call. On Oct. 6, it defaulted on a $74M loan on the 691K SF Fashion Outlets of Niagara Falls in New York. On Nov. 2, it defaulted on a $325M loan on the 974K SF Fresno Fashion Fair mall in California. Macerich had previously announced a $76M default on Twenty Ninth Street, an open-air lifestyle center in Boulder, Colorado. Macerich executives did not offer additional details on the defaults. “I can't really talk too much about these mortgages that are in default,” Macerich CEO Jackson Hsieh said on the call. “Lenders are listening or whatever, it's not very fair. So let's just say we are in default. We're still having conversations, and we'll let you know when we got more to say, but that's what it is.” Macerich is in the midst of a multiquarter plan to rebalance its portfolio and improve its balance sheet by offloading a number of underperforming properties, with a goal of selling or giving back $300M to $400M in assets and land. The company is on track to achieve that objective this year and has sold about $290M worth of dispositions this year to date, Macerich Chief Financial Officer Daniel Swanstrom said on the call. Macerich reported a $16.7M loss in the quarter, though that was an improvement from the same period last year, when it reported an approximately $90M loss, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission . The Niagara outlet mall is on the disposition list. Its loan has been modified twice already, including a three-year extension when it originally matured in 2020 and another after missing its 2023 maturity date, CoStar News reported. Its occupancy has dropped as low as 60% in recent years. The Fresno mall is not on the list of properties for sale. There, Macerich is in the middle of large-scale renovations to public spaces and is adding new tenants, including a $22M Dick's House of Sport, which is expected to open by mid-2028. The mall's special servicer is negotiating terms that would temporarily hold off enforcement of the loan default. Macerich is also still acquiring properties. On its earnings call, Hsieh teased an off-market mall purchase that is under contract now and should close by the end of the year. Malls broadly have been on a rebound. Values were up 13% over the past year, more than double the increase in all CRE prices, The Wall Street Journal reported in September . items.description: Oppenheimer & Co. is taking over six floors of a Financial District office tower. Google Maps 32 Old Slip in Manhattan's Financial District, where landlord RXR inked a 220K SF lease with investment firm Oppenheimer this week The investment bank signed for 220K SF at RXR ’s 32 Old Slip , a 36-story, 1.1M SF skyscraper, with plans to begin its move-in during the first quarter of 2028. The company plans to relocate from a 270K SF space at 85 Broad St., a spokesperson for JLL, which represented the tenant, told Bisnow . “Oppenheimer’s commitment to 32 Old Slip speaks to the enduring appeal of Lower Manhattan and the continued evolution of its office market,” William Elder , RXR’s executive vice president and manager of the landlord’s New York City division, said in a statement. RXR, which paid $675M for the property in 2015, said it will jointly invest around $66M into the space with Oppenheimer to support a renovation and fit-out led by Gensler. “Our new headquarters at 32 Old Slip in Lower Manhattan reaffirms our commitment to the area,” Oppenheimer President and CEO Robert Lowenthal said in a statement. “This move is an investment in our culture, bringing our teams together on six floors with modern technology and a dedicated space to welcome clients.” The deal will keep more than 1,000 jobs in FiDi , according to Gov. Kathy Hochul . New York state’s economic development agency, Empire State Development , is providing the company with a $3.2M capital grant. “This commitment sends a clear message that there is no better place to do business than New York,” Hochul said in a statement . “We have the talent, the access to global markets and resources companies need to compete, innovate and grow.” JLL ’s Matt Astrachan, Mitchell Konsker and Steven Bauer represented Oppenheimer in the deal, while RXR’s Daniel Birney and Heidi Steinegger represented the landlord in-house. Despite NYC’s status as a financial powerhouse, Downtown Manhattan has lagged behind Midtown and Midtown South in the battle to attract tenants since the pandemic due to its high stock of Class-B and C buildings. items.title: Pro-housing coalition presses Senate on BAAJA permitting reforms
items.description: A coalition of national housing organizations, homebuilders and 58 local pro-housing groups is urging Senate leaders to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), arguing its permitting reforms could sharply cut timelines and costs for federally supported housing. In a letter to key Senate committee leaders, co-led by Inclusive Abundance Action and summarized in a public statement Monday, the coalition backs the housing provisions in BAAJA (S. 5653), the Senate’s bipartisan permitting reform package. The groups say the bill could “transform how quickly federally supported housing gets built,” even though most public attention on BAAJA has focused on its energy and infrastructure impacts rather than its potential to accelerate affordable and multifamily projects. What BAAJA could change for housing Today, federally assisted affordable and multifamily housing typically faces National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) reviews and National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) reviews that do not apply to most private-market projects. Affordable housing developers report delays of a year or more to clear environmental review and up to three months just to document that a project is exempt, according to the letter. The coalition highlights several housing-specific changes in BAAJA that it says would help the following areas: Streamlined federal reviews: Projects using federal grants, loans or loan guarantees that are not primarily preservation-focused would no longer automatically trigger a federal historic preservation review, the groups say. The bill would also narrow and streamline when NEPA applies, allow qualified state or Tribal reviews to substitute for federal review, expand categorical exclusions and set clearer timelines. Potential savings per project: Streamlined Clean Water Act reviews could save up to an estimated $425,000 per project, according to materials cited by the coalition. Faster deployment of HUD dollars: At least $10 billion a year in U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development funding could move more quickly under the bill’s changes, including Community Development Block Grants (CDBG), HOME funds, public housing capital and operating funds, and HUD loan programs, the coalition says. Building on prior reforms: BAAJA would extend and expand permitting reforms already enacted in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act , which Congress passed earlier this year with bipartisan majorities. For developers and public housing agencies that rely on layered federal funds, the changes would primarily affect front-end approvals rather than long-term compliance. But the groups argue that shaving months off NEPA and related reviews would materially improve feasibility for marginal projects and reduce soft costs. Who is backing the bill? The signatories span national trade groups, think tanks and local YIMBY organizations. Organizations named in the public statement include: National Association of Home Builders National Community Development Association Council of State Community Development Agencies National Housing & Rehabilitation Association National Association of Home Builders Institute for Progress Niskanen Center Center for Public Enterprise Action Fund Up for Growth Action YIMBY Action They are joined by 58 local pro-housing or “Yes In My Backyard” (YIMBY) groups from across the country, according to the coalition’s announcement. The attached letter, addressed to Senate committee leadership, urges lawmakers to preserve and enact the housing-related provisions as part of any final permitting package. Why this matters The push around BAAJA highlights a growing focus on federal permitting as a bottleneck for subsidized housing, separate from local zoning and entitlement risk. For developers and public agencies, the proposed changes could mean: Shorter and more predictable federal review timelines on projects using HUD and other federal funds. Greater ability to rely on state or Tribal environmental review processes instead of duplicative federal NEPA reviews. Lower predevelopment and legal costs tied to environmental and historic preservation compliance. Related More: Homebuilders Housing Policy

items.title: Lenders face more TCPA suits despite litigation trend easing
items.description: Lenders face more TCPA suits despite litigation trend easing By Andrew Martinez CloseText About Andrew twitter andrewomartinez mailto andrew.martinez@arizent.com linkedin andrewomartinez Published November 09, 2026, 6:00 a.m. EST | Updated November 09, 2026, 6:03 a.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email What's at Stake: More lenders face penalties of up to $1,500 per "willful" violation of the law for alleged mortgage solicitations. Supporting Data: Federal Telephone Consumer Protection Act lawsuits against all defendants are down on a monthly basis, but still up 13% on the year. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Consumers are hitting mortgage lenders with spam call lawsuits as fast as they can swat them away. Seven more origination shops have been sued for Telephone Consumer Protection Act claims since August, after dozens of lenders were sued for alleged violations this year. That litigation has poured in despite many of those earlier mortgage cases being settled or dismissed outright. Processing Content Companies can run afoul of the law if they send two or more unwanted phone calls in a 12-month period to a customer on the national Do Not Call Registry. While some of the latest lawsuits allege that lenders hit that small threshold, other consumers describe a harassment campaign of mortgage solicitations spanning months. "Consumers in the United States are united in their disdain for unsolicited marketing calls and texts," wrote attorney Max Morgan of The Weitz Firm on behalf of one of the latest plaintiffs, in a statement Friday. "Congress has warned telemarketers about the consequences of disturbing people without their permission." Penalties for each call can range from $500 to $1,500 for a willful and knowing violation. Real estate firms have paid out massive settlements in past years in TCPA cases, although a mortgage lender hasn't agreed to a large public settlement in a case this year. Who's being sued? Some of the latest real estate companies named as defendants in recent months have already been sued this year. They include: Barrett Financial Group , with $9.96 billion in volume year-to-date per Modex; eMortgage Funding , with $769 million in volume; GFS Home Loans , with $872 million in volume; Mortgage Pros , with $1.22 billion in volume; Mutual of Omaha Mortgage , with $8.2 billion in volume; Swift Home Loans , with $3.2 billion in volume. A plaintiff also sued Premier Agency Real Estate, a Southern California-based brokerage with 27 agents. Several attorneys for both plaintiffs and defendants, and company representatives, declined to comment on the pending litigation. The cases are structured similarly, although the number of combined mortgage solicitations via text messages and phone calls varies. Christopher Laccione accuses Swift of sending him at least two dozen home loan solicitations, despite his pleas that he wasn't interested. He accused the alleged Swift callers of failing to identify their affiliation. "Upon information and belief, SHL trained its representatives to be evasive because SHL knew it was violating the TCPA and various state laws and did not want to reveal its identity to minimize complaints and litigation," attorneys for Laccione, including Max Morgan, wrote. In a motion to dismiss last month, Swift argued that the plaintiff could only prove one of the phone calls came from a Swift representative, and that the consumer did not reply "stop" to text messages offering him to end outreach. An attorney and representative for the company didn't respond to requests for comment. Litigation exposure easing? In some recent motions to dismiss, lenders have begun to cite a landmark TCPA decision this summer, in which an appellate court held that the law doesn't cover text messages. None of the recent class action suits rely on sole accusations of text message outreach. Of the earlier cases filed against the industry this year, lenders have reached resolutions in at least a dozen of those filings. Tomo Mortgage and LendingTree reached undisclosed settlements in respective TCPA cases this year, while other lenders filed joint motions to dismiss with plaintiffs that did not describe settlements. The torrid pace of TCPA litigation against businesses nationwide has slowed somewhat. While federal TCPA complaints are still up around 13% on the year through October, their monthly pace has fallen, according to WebRecon . September's 191 nationwide TCPA complaints were down 27% from the same time last year. Andrew Martinez Reporter Andrew Martinez joined National Mortgage News in January 2022. items.title: 'Certainty Will Be The Buzzword': Stability, Not Sea Change, For CRE Post-Midterm
items.description: The implications of an overwhelming Democratic midterm victory reverberated through markets in the second half of last week, reflecting skittishness among investors and business leaders over fears about the impact on the largest driver of today's economy: data center growth. Despite these initial shocks, there is a quiet expectation that a Democratic Congress will help bring calm to a period of significant economic volatility stemming in part from the unpredictable policymaking that has emerged during President Donald Trump 's second term. “Maybe ‘uncertainty’ was the buzzword of the last year, and hopefully ‘certainty’ will be the buzzword going forward,” said Jeff DeBoer , CEO of the Washington, D.C.-based trade group The Real Estate Roundtable . “We're much more certain that we're not going to wake up every day and have another wild fluctuation in some sort of policy.” Unsplash/Sebastian Schuster That semblance of certainty won't be a panacea, however. Major relief from the ubiquitous issues for commercial real estate today, including higher costs, low labor availability and expensive debt, is unlikely to come from the new Congress because those issues are closely tied to Trump's executive actions and powers. But housing affordability, the economy more generally and data centers were on the ballot in races around the country, where the results have set the stage for a string of policy debates that will hit landlords and investors. “If you look back in history, there are a number of examples where a great amount of very positive legislation has been done when there's divided government,” DeBoer said. “I'm not one who says, ‘Put your feet up, nothing's going to happen, we're in for gridlock.’ I think there's going to be some significant legislation.” Stock traders initially reacted positively to the midterm results, with all three major indexes climbing, but the mood changed Thursday. A massive sell-off focused on tech stocks but spread marketwide sucked $2.5T in market value out of the Nasdaq and pushed the index into correction territory. By Friday, the dust had settled and markets opened by gaining back some of Thursday’s losses. Investors are trying to reprice their bets on the pace of the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out as they weigh the prospect of a Congress that is more skeptical of the major tech firms’ plans and a wave of local fervor against data centers that drove voters to the polls. AI and data centers emerged as a key political flashpoint, with more than half of respondents telling an NBC exit poll that it was a crucial or major factor in their decision to vote in the midterms. Across statewide races and referendums, voters roundly supported measures putting limits on data center development in more than 40 local ballot measures . “This election, whether federally or on the local level, was influenced by data centers,” said Commercial Real Estate Development Association CEO Marc Selvitelli. “This was the rare bipartisan issue that was out there right now.” The economy emerged as the top issue for voters headed into the election after the U.S. war with Iran drove up energy costs and added to already elevated inflation. The president’s tariffs are also contributing to the rising costs, but the Democratic sweep in Congress still has limited reach into trade policy that’s coming directly from the White House. "The swing in Congress, the results of the election, are very unlikely to have a significant impact on the president's trade agenda and the tariffs that are in place," Blake Harden, managing director for trade policy at ​ Ernst & Young 's Washington Council office, told Reuters . "This is because there is so much trade authority within the executive branch that's been delegated by Congress." Unsplash/Jesse Paul Democrats have floated the idea of changing the tariff laws the president is relying on to impose his protectionist trade regime, but the party would need to win over some Republicans because it remains short of a veto-proof majority. They’re also working on a plan to roll back Trump’s tariffs directed at Canada, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday. “The midterm election results are unlikely to materially influence commercial real estate performance,” Cushman & Wakefield analysts wrote in a postelection report . A divided government adds some degree of fiscal policy stability that “should be calming for markets,” although the U.S. war in Iran and the downstream impacts on prices and inflation remain the greatest “swing factor for inflation and rates,” they wrote. The election was at least in part a referendum on the war in Iran, according to Hans Nordby , executive managing director of research and investment analytics at Transwestern . “And it was a ‘no’ vote,” Nordby wrote in an email to Bisnow on Friday. “The new Congress could defund the war or otherwise force a withdrawal. If that were to happen, it would seem likely that oil prices could retreat to prewar levels, which would put downward pressure on inflation.” The war and its economic fallout, particularly on the price of oil, has been a thorn in CRE's side since it broke out in February. The rising cost of oil has contributed to overall inflation remaining elevated, which in turn has kept borrowing rates higher. Yields for 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds , a key benchmark rate for all sorts of debt costs, notched lower following the midterms after climbing above 5% in October before retreating, shedding 6 basis points Wednesday and continuing to trade below 4.9% through Friday. The shift in Congress likely sets the stage for bitter political fights between Trump and Democrats, some of whom have pledged to launch investigations into the White House. items.title: Casino Mogul Steve Wynn Sells His $70 Million Central Park Condo as Manhattan Luxury Market Heats Up
items.description: Casino billionaire Steve Wynn has finally unloaded his Central Park duplex penthouse, making it the top luxury sale of a record-breaking week in Manhattan . The mogul's prewar condo at 50 Central Park South—first listed in 2022 for $90 million, the most expensive in the country at the time—eventually saw its price drop to $70 million. Even at this steep discount, it still took two years for the condo to find a taker. The duplex went into contract last week with Serena Boardman of Sotheby's International Realty as the listing agent (co-exclusive with Deborah Grubman of Corcoran). The sale means the casino magnate failed to turn a profit on the 10,875-square-foot condo. But given that, according to Forbes , Wynn is worth $4.3 billion, he likely isn't sweating it too much. The Billionaires Row duplex takes up the 30th and 31st floors within the 36-story Ritz-Carlton Residences, formerly the Hotel St. Moritz, which opened in 1930. The top 12 floors are the private homes. Loading... A luxury condo on the 30th and 31st floors at 50 Central Park South overlooking the park listed $70,000,000 was last week's top sale in Manhattan. Realtor.com The penthouse, formerly owned by real estate developer Christopher M. Jeffries , comes with an esteemed pedigree. It was Jeffries' Millennium Partners that purchased the Emory Roth –designed building in 1999 and reimagined it along with the Ritz-Carlton Hotel Co. Jeffries was once married to Princess Yasmin Aga Khan , the only child of Prince Aly Khan and movie legend Rita Hayworth . Yet the real selling point of the duplex is its sweeping Central Park views. With floors that aren't too high, from the vantage of the 45-foot long terrace, it feels as if one is sitting in the famed park's trees—a "bird's-eye perspective," as the listing puts it. Another terrace along the western wall stretches 28 feet. With three bedrooms, four full baths, and two half-baths, the prewar unit features 10 grandly arched windows, a marble staircase, 15-foot coffered ceilings, and a living room that used to be the St. Moritz ballroom. Modern touches include a chef's kitchen; a breakfast room with its own terrace; a primary bedroom with Central Park views, en suite bathroom, gym, and dressing room; a staff room with laundry; and a library. Loading... A terrace facing Central Park gives extraordinary "bird's-eye" views and likely clinched the sale. Realtor.com As the condo sits atop the flagship Ritz-Carlton hotel, it comes with access to the amenities of the global luxury name, including the La Prairie spa and health club, a business center, the Contour Bar and Lounge, in-room dining services, and housekeeping services. The unit has $31,362 in monthly dues on top of $15,500 in taxes. As for why a property offering such grandeur may have taken so long to move, luxury broker Michael Reisor with Compass-affiliated Reisor.Team, who is familiar with the building, says, "Properties like this are wonderful but specific. There's a more limited buyer pool." Despite the park views and architectural significance, it's still a century-old building, and buyers at this price range have their pick. However, "when buyers at this level want prewar charm and detail, there is only one way to get it authentically, and that is to buy of that era," he says. "Are there people in droves wanting to pay at this level for prewar? No, but there are people who do. It's usually a more sophisticated buyer. "They want that, 'This is classic New York .'" Loading... The unit has plenty of prewar charm, including arched windows and coffered 15-foot ceilings. Realtor.com The final price isn't yet known, but Reisor says, "We can assume it was right around [the ask price], if not right on." The buyer hasn't been revealed, and listing agent Boardman did not return a call for comment. One unique aspect of the 50 Central Park prewar is that it is a condo, not a co-op. Prewar buildings—built between the late 1880s and 1939—are typically co-ops. In general, condos outsell co-ops each week—and after two weeks of the gap between them being slim, for the week ending Nov. 8, condos were far ahead, 34 contracts versus 7. Co-ops tend to be cheaper, with an average ask of $8.6 million last week versus $10.5 million for condos, according to Olshan Realty . Another unusual feature of the sprawling duplex is that it has only three bedrooms. Often condos at this scale have expanded to four or more. Last week's top sale, a $31 million penthouse condo at 111 Murray St. in Tribeca, had five bedrooms. Loading... Many of the windows within the unit come with sweeping Central Park views. Realtor.com "It's more of a psychological sticking point than an actual need," Reisor says of a high-end buyer's desire for plentiful bedrooms. "They think, 'At a certain price, I should be overflowing with bedrooms.' Even if they never need them." Whoever snapped up the trophy unit likely wanted to be in that particular building, which is low-density, has only 11 private residences inside of a global luxury brand, and comes with a glamorous history and illustrious architect. "It could be someone high-profile," Reisor speculates of the mystery buyer. "Someone high-profile would want something like this." Manhattan luxury is still booming The Wynn sale was one of a slew of high-end contracts last week, with 45 signed, a big leap of 11 over the week before, and the biggest luxury sales week for the entire year. Of that, an astonishing 14 sales were priced over $10 million. The New York City pied-à-terre tax doesn't seem to be squeezing the top end of the market. items.title: Housing Week Ahead: Hottest Markets, Inflation, and Existing-Home Sales
items.description: The coming week brings a steady stream of new reports from the Realtor.com economics team, as well as a number of key indicators for the housing market. On Monday, senior economist Anthony Smith published the October Luxury Report , which looks at pockets of growth where luxury prices are still rising. On Tuesday, ahead of Veterans Day, we honor America’s military service members and veterans with a report on Veterans Affairs loans . Senior economist Jiayi Xu explores what they are and how they help with homeownership. On Wednesday, senior economist Hannah Jones examines how the lock-in effect has evolved and where today’s homeowners with a mortgage face larger or smaller payment shocks if they are thinking about moving. On Thursday, Hannah is back to examine what the first full week of November data reveals about the housing market, and on Friday, Hannah publishes the October Hottest Markets report, which identifies the markets where homes are moving the fastest and getting the most attention from online shoppers. Turning to the economic indicators that will be released, we’ll see the consumer price index reading on inflation as well as mortgage rates and existing-home sales. Inflation has run above the Fed’s target, 2% growth in headline PCE, for 5.5 years, and it’s clear from exit polls that the cost of living was very much on the mind of voters in last week’s election. This week, we’ll see the first inflation reading for October from the consumer price index, which was up sharply in September largely due to higher energy prices. I’m expecting the annual inflation reading to be similarly high in October even if the month-to-month momentum wanes a bit. Although inflation remains elevated, mortgage rates could continue to ebb. Last week the 30-year fixed mortgage rate, according to Freddie Mac , dropped to 7.18% as the 10-year hovered near 4.9%. Late in the week, the 10-year yield dropped further as uncertainty over artificial intelligence investments led to a pullback in stocks. Even if the 10-year were to remain at 4.9%, it has adjusted faster than mortgage rates, so I think there is room for spread compression that could help nudge rates lower, which will help late-season home shoppers. The last indicator of the week is existing-home sales data from the National Association of Realtors®. That October home sales data is likely to be very disappointing. Mortgage rates rose sharply in the month, and NAR’s pending home sales hit a series record low in September, while Realtor.com housing data suggests that the buyer pullback continued into October . I’m watching to see if the pullback is sufficient to push months supply even higher. For full reports, the Market Clock, and raw housing data, visit realtor.com/research .
