items.title: What Would Losing the Mavs and Stars Cost Downtown? An Economist Answers Your Questions.
items.description: Live Poll Five thousand dollars. For anyone who's tried to get a table at a restaurant or bar around the American Airlines Center before a Mavericks or Stars game, that number is hard to swallow. Last week, D CEO reported Cal Poly economist Joseph S. Kuehn’s estimate that games generate about $5,000 in additional spending per contest across businesses within a quarter-mile of the AAC. That’s the estimated increase over spending on non-game days—not the total fans spend. Many of you had questions—plenty of them. On LinkedIn, Instagram, and X, people pointed to packed bars, pregame dinners, and their own substantial tabs. So, I touched base with Kuehn again to press him on what his data captures, which business benefits the most, and whether looking farther from the arena changes the picture. Introducing: The POWER 50 Our new program spotlights North Texas executives under 50 shaping the region’s future. Nominations are open through Nov. 13. Learn More A packed bar before a game starts tells you people are spending money. What it doesn’t tell you is how much they would have spent in the neighborhood if there were no game. That’s the comparison at the heart of Kuehn’s research—and the question I went back to him to better understand. His answers add context and nuance to the story posted last week —and include another estimate that shocked me. This conversation has been edited for brevity and clarity. D CEO: Where did the idea for your study originate? JOSEPH S. KUEHN: "Economists have been saying for a long time that there’s not too much of an economic impact from stadiums, even large sporting events like bringing in the Olympics or World Cup. There’s some, but it’s not enough to justify the large spending that cities do for these events and stadiums. "But I wanted to look specifically at what impact there was day to day, game to game. I had this cool credit card transaction data—basically a panel of individual credit card and debit card transactions. It allows me to look at where these individuals spend on game days versus non-game days. "What I find interesting is that you see this very different result between NBA and NHL games versus NFL and MLB games. I think a lot has to do with where those stadiums are located. Hockey and basketball arenas tend to be in these urban cores where people are already spending money. So you’re not going to see a big boost, whereas with an NFL stadium on the outskirts of a city, people are going to go there for the game and spend more money there. I think that’s one striking difference. "I think what’s also interesting is that while the overall effect—in Dallas at the AAC, it’s $5,000 within a quarter-mile radius, but it’s different in other places—is kind of small around the country, there are differences between the types of establishments. Restaurants and bars do get boosts. "At the other shops around those areas, people start to avoid them on game day. That can offset some of the larger effects you get at restaurants and bars. Bars especially do get a big boost around game time. "I know these results are always somewhat controversial, but I think this fits within the long line of research in economics that hasn’t shown a lot of large economic impact. Even longer-run studies that look over years and years at the impacts that moving a team to a new stadium is going to show a lot of shifts in spending, but not necessarily big increases and big economic impacts." D CEO: Dallas is unique in that we are a very car-dependent city; it's sprawling. What does your Dallas data say if we extend out another quarter-mile? Say, all businesses within a half-mile of the AAC? I realize you state in your paper that the further away we get from the arena, the less certain you are that it's directly correlated to the game. KUEHN : "Dallas actually does have a bigger impact a quarter- to a half-mile away, which is unusual compared to other cities. Maybe that goes to what you're saying about Dallas. But the quarter- to half-mile area has a larger impact. Usually, you see a steady decline as you go farther out. "The standard error is a little larger, so there’s a little more uncertainty, and it’s harder to pinpoint exactly. But for restaurants and bars, I’m seeing about a $10,000 increase per game day in that area. Lodging is another $10,000 or so, but then there are some big losses for retailers. Overall, retail tends to not do so well." D CEO: Do you mind sharing which restaurants, bars, or retailers are encapsulated in your data? KUEHN : "The big gainers are Capital Grille , House of Blues Restaurant and Bar, Happiest Hour , Moxies , and Fearings at the Ritz-Carlton. They seem to do very well. Then, on the other side, the restaurant that does poorly on game days is Hero .” D CEO: What? Hero is on your list of restaurants where spending goes down on a game day? KUEHN : "Yes. By my estimates, about $480 less on a game day." D CEO: I'm not sure how that is possible. People were appalled by your numbers at the start. I think that will be appalling as well. It is to me. So, as you know, the Stars are trying to build a new arena in Plano , and the Mavericks are trying to build one in far North Dallas . For these cities and areas considering new arenas, is it really worth it? What’s your take? KUEHN : [Pauses] "I mean, no. But I do think—not just in the Dallas area, but across the country—there are very localized impacts that can be important to that immediate area, especially if you’re operating a restaurant or bar there. “We might be talking about small average numbers, but for those restaurants and bars in the immediate area, I think there is a substantial impact that is important. items.title: Treasury rally gets new boost as election hammers AI trade
items.description: Treasury rally gets new boost as election hammers AI trade By Michael MacKenzie and Ye Xie Published November 09, 2026, 9:50 a.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Wall Street sees the Treasury market emerging as a winner from the Democratic landslide in the US midterm elections, giving traders another reason to rethink this year's sharp selloff. Processing Content The party's sweep of Congress was seized upon by bond bulls after tech stocks tumbled on speculation the political shift will tap the brakes on an artificial-intelligence investment boom that's been fueling economic growth, fanning inflation and pushing up interest rates as companies flood the market with debt to finance it. A politically divided government will also prevent President Donald Trump from passing any major tax or spending bills, easing some of the market's angst about an annual budget deficit that's hit $2 trillion, equivalent to roughly 6% of the economy. READ MORE: Post-midterm rate rally: Prime pipeline borrowers to act now And oil prices tumbled on speculation the Republican defeat will hasten the end of the Iran war, whose energy shock unleashed the bond market selloff eight months ago. The response to the elections extended a nearly monthlong Treasury rally that pushed 10-year yields down to nearly 4.8%, more than a half-percentage-point below the early October peak. The market largely held its weekly gain even after Friday's Labor Department report showed that job growth accelerated significantly last month. Treasuries were little changed on Monday morning, as investors weighed a drop in oil prices and a rebound in US stocks. "AI's been the biggest contributor to nominal GDP, so any kind of stumble probably helps the bond market," said Scott DiMaggio, head of fixed income at AllianceBernstein. "You have the insurance, that if things wobble, we have a great room to move lower in rates." The bond market's rapid turnaround echoes the one that erupted at the end of 2023, when yields tumbled sharply after the Federal Reserve wrapped up a cycle of interest-rate hikes. But the scope of the rally has given some analysts pause because the Fed is currently expected resume raising rates next month as inflation continues to run well above its 2% target. READ MORE: Lenders turn to cuts, AI as strong jobs point to rate hikes Moreover, the stock market has been dogged by worries about an AI bubble off and on for years, only to rebound as companies keep plowing money into the technology and investors swoop in to buy the dips. "Unless stocks continue to sell off violently, I think we have come too far too fast," said John Briggs, head of US rates strategy at Natixis North America. The bond market will face its next test on Tuesday, when the consumer price index for October is released. Economists expect it to show a slowdown in inflation from a month earlier, though year-over-year figures won't be released because the government shutdown last year hobbled data collection. The Treasury Department will also hold its quarterly refunding auctions this week. It will begin with a 3-year sale on Monday, followed by 10-year notes on Tuesday and 30-year bonds Thursday. Cash trading in the US bond market will be closed on Wednesday because of the Veterans Day holiday. The surging supply of new debt to cover the federal budget deficit is likely to continue to weigh on the market, as will lingering uncertainty about the Iran war, how much further the Fed will hike interest rates, and what policies the new Democratic Congress will embrace. But given how high yields had risen — and the new political checks on Trump's power — investors still see it as a good chance to lock elevated bond yields. "Fixed income is a pretty attractive proposition here," said Neil Sutherland, portfolio manager at Schroder Investment Management. "A lot of the things which are vexing markets today will be behind us" in the next six to 12 months, he said, "which on balance will be supportive for the bond market." Michael MacKenzie and Ye Xie Bloomberg News

items.title: What View Homes' rebrand says about Gandhi’s operating overhaul
items.description: Seven months into her effort to transform View Homes from a loose collection of regional builders into a cohesive enterprise, CEO Natasha Gandhi has drawn a line between the company's past and its ambitions. A newly unified brand makes that promise visible. Now Gandhi and her team must overdeliver on it. View Homes announced Monday a new corporate brand identity, unifying its formerly distinct Aspen View, Desert View, Horizon View and View Homes operations under one name. The change spans five divisions across Colorado, New Mexico and Texas and marks a milestone in the operational transformation Gandhi began after becoming CEO in March 2026. The announcement also comes one week after View's parent, Hunt Companies , joined with global investment manager Wafra to launch Strata Land Partners , a new land-financing platform led by former Landsea Homes president Michael Forsum. Together, these developments offer a clearer view of Hunt's expanding ambitions in U.S. residential construction and development. In an exclusive interview with HousingWire TBD , Gandhi said the branding initiative is part of a broader effort to prepare View for growth, strengthen operating standards, and compete across more markets and homebuyer segments. "We want to be a premium builder, and by premium, it's not that we're unaffordable," Gandhi said. "It just means that we want to be the best in every price point that we're out there, we want to be the best in every market that we build in." One brand, one operating standard Hunt acquired full ownership of View Homes in 2025, inheriting an established 35-year-old homebuilding business whose regional operations had developed distinct identities, systems and operating practices. When Gandhi arrived in March, she found an organization with strong local relationships and experienced teams, but lacking the consistent management processes, reporting systems, and enterprise infrastructure needed to support the growth Hunt envisioned. As The Builder's Daily reported in October , Gandhi's initial work focused on leadership changes, clearer accountability, more disciplined sales concessions, selective land investment, and a comprehensive review of enterprise technology. The new branding establishes four standards intended to apply across the organization: exceptional customer experience, people-first leadership, design-forward homes, and premium quality across price points. "I felt like previously, we had different standards in different markets, but now with this new brand, it really sets the stage," Gandhi said. "These four pillars are something that is now going to be operationally executed in all our markets." The challenge is to translate those commitments into consistent performance without compromising the local knowledge and customer relationships that have made View's regional businesses successful. For a multiregional homebuilder, Gandhi notes, that means more than consistent signage and marketing. It requires shared expectations for product quality, customer service, sales execution, and management accountability, supported by reliable information and operating systems. The work behind the promise Gandhi is candid that the transformation remains unfinished. "This is just the start of our growth journey," she said. "I will tell you, we're not there yet, but we're on the path of getting there." The branding initiative has prompted further scrutiny of the operational capabilities needed to support the company's ambitions to up its game. Gandhi acknowledged that View's enterprise resource planning systems and website are not yet up to par. A builder seeking to expand across markets needs timely, consistent information on sales, margins, construction costs, inventory, and land commitments. Without it, management cannot easily compare performance across divisions or make informed decisions about capital allocation. Gandhi previously outlined a 12-to-18-month enterprise technology implementation, along with efforts to standardize sales concessions and improve the quality of operating data. Those initiatives remain important to the company's ability to scale. View has also raised the bar in its home merchandising across markets and is developing products designed to reach beyond its traditional entry-level customer base. The objective is to preserve affordability where that remains the market opportunity while broadening View's appeal to move-up buyers and customers seeking greater design and product differentiation. The Hunt capital connection The transformation is unfolding amid difficult housing economics. Slower sales, persistent affordability pressures, and costly incentives continue to strain builder margins, while land acquisition and development require substantial capital commitments long before homes generate revenue. Hunt's ownership gives View access to a larger real estate investment organization and a longer-term investment perspective. Its recent partnership with Wafra to establish Strata Land Partners adds another potentially valuable capability. Strata launched with projects comprising approximately 1,300 single-family lots and a mandate to provide flexible land-financing solutions for public and private homebuilders and developers nationwide. Forsum has described the platform as a capital partner "built by builders, for builders," emphasizing the need to understand the operational risks and financial requirements of homebuilding businesses. Gandhi confirmed that View and Strata are already discussing opportunities to work together. "We are actually already exploring opportunities to where Strata and [View] can partner together," she said. "There's definitely opportunity and conversations already in place." She did not identify specific transactions or financing structures under review. items.title: NAR moves from survival to ‘showing receipts’ on member value
items.description: A little over two years have passed since Nykia Wright was named permanent CEO of the National Association of Realtors (NAR). Her tenure as the CEO of the nation’s largest trade association began in a period of unprecedented turmoil for the over 100 year old organization. During an address to NAR’s board of directors Monday morning at NAR’s 2026 NXT conference and board meeting, Wright attributed much of the association's success in navigating this turmoil to 2025 NAR President Kevin Sears , who began his term early, in January 2024 after Tracy Kasper’s resignation. “I wanted to remind us just how much leadership matters. The two years of Kevin Sears's leadership was defined by leading us through never before experienced turbulence,” Wright, a HousingWire Woman of Influence , said. “Not just the turbulence of survival versus extinction, which is singularly difficult on its own, but also cultural turbulence. And under his leadership, we set the groundwork for what we were promising we were going to do if we were given the chance.” Another Kevin takes the lead For the past year , however, it was 2026 NAR President Kevin Brown, who was tasked with carrying out the plan, namely the first year of NAR’s 2026-2028 strategic plan. “Kevin Brown's leadership was defined by the showing of actual receipts. January 1st of this year represented the official starting of the clock for our three-year strategic plan that was authored by the membership. They asked, and he began to deliver,” Wright said. Under Brown’s guidance this year, Wright said that this was the first year NAR made contact with all 450+ MLSs across the country. Back to business In taking the helm from Sears last fall, Brown said his primary focus was on getting Realtors “ back to business ” by helping members “navigate the issues that impact their day-to-day business like financing, inventory, insurance, zoning restrictions and other barriers to home and property ownership.” This translated into tackling a variety of challenges. These efforts came to fruition this week when the association approved four MLS policy recommendations that increase MLSs’ options to claim copyright in listing content, expand local flexibility on data feeds, clarify permissible uses of MLS data and update qualifications for NAR’s MLS Committee. items.title: loanDepot's Q3 loss grows while it chases 2027 break-even
items.description: loanDepot widened its net loss in the third quarter of 2026 as it sold mortgage servicing rights (MSRs), repurchased debt and leaned into higher-margin products. The California-based nonbank lender reported a $29 million net loss in Q3, compared with a $7 million loss in the prior quarter, according to its earnings release Monday. Founder and CEO Anthony Hsieh told analysts that the quarter was challenged by unexpectedly higher interest rates but said the company remains focused on gaining market share despite depressed volumes. “Getting over the seasonality of Q4 and Q1, and of course not knowing where the market will end up next year, but if it stays at this level, we are very confident that we'll get to a break even of profitability by first half or mid next year,” Hsieh said. loanDepot originated $7.05 billion in mortgages in the third quarter, down 12% from the prior quarter but up 7.8% year over year. Purchase loans made up more than 61% of total volume. On a unit basis, originations rose 7% quarter over quarter, helped by the company’s expansion into home equity products. Management said loanDepot estimates it ranked among the top three nonbank home equity lenders in the third quarter based on volume, a shift that helped push gain-on-sale margin to 399 basis points, up 54 basis points from the second quarter. “Since my return last year, we increased origination volume by 8%, grew unit volume by 33%, increased purchase volume by 10%, improved return on marketing by 14%, and reduced our cost to produce by 16%,” Hsieh said. “These results reflect the success of our ongoing efforts to diversify revenue sources, increase operating efficiency, and improve the scalability of our platform.” The company now expects its productivity and efficiency initiatives to deliver $25 million in annualized cost savings through the remainder of 2026, more than double the previous estimate of $12 million. MSR sales fund deleveraging push loanDepot continued to shrink its balance sheet and reduce debt through MSR sales in the quarter. The company closed the sale of $10 billion in agency MSRs and agreed to sell an additional $9 billion in government MSRs, a transaction expected to close in October. After these moves, loanDepot’s servicing portfolio stood at $115.7 billion at the end of the quarter. Proceeds were used to repurchase $87 million of senior notes at an average price of 88% of par. Chief Financial Officer David Hayes said the combination of MSR sales and debt repurchases reduced net debt obligations by about $114 million, strengthened liquidity and improved financial flexibility. Even with those steps, leverage remains elevated. Debt obligations, net to total equity, were 6.5x at the end of the quarter, up from 4.8x a year earlier. Hayes said the company is working “actively” to address nearing debt maturities and is pursuing financing options to refinance or extend with financing counterparties ahead of 2027 bond maturities. He did not provide more details during the calls with analysts. Guidance Looking to the fourth quarter of 2026, loanDepot guided to origination volume between $4.5 billion and $6.5 billion, implying potentially lower production than Q3. However, it expects gain-on-sale margin between 315 basis points and 355 basis points. Management framed the outlook as a continuation of the pivot toward more profitable products, a larger purchase footprint and a leaner cost base in the face of persistent rate pressure. “While elevated interest rates remain a headwind for mortgage demand, we believe the actions we have taken to diversify our product offerings, expand our purchase market presence, improve efficiency, strengthen margins, and optimize our balance sheet have positioned loanDepot to emerge from this cycle as a stronger and more competitive company,” Hsieh said in a statement. “We remain focused on growing market share, improving profitability, and creating long-term value for our shareholders.” Related More: Earnings loanDepot

items.title: NAR membership proves more resilient than expected, topping 1.46 million
items.description: It is no secret that the National Association of Realtors (NAR) had a challenging few years. From facing a sexual harassment scandal , navigating the commission lawsuits and the implementation of the resulting settlement, to looking to create a more accountable and responsible version of the trade group , NAR has experienced its fair share of growing pains. But, when it comes to the association’s financials, 2026 was far better than anticipated. In an update at NAR’s 2026 NXT Board of Directors meeting by NAR’s 2026 Treasurer Craig Sanford, it was revealed that at the end of September, the association had 1,469,127 members, 22% better than the 1.2 million members the association had budgeted for and just 1.5% lower than membership a year ago. In addition, Sanford said membership renewals for 2027 are tracking in line with where they were in 2026. Revenue from membership dues accounted for roughly $220 million of the more than $250 million in revenue NAR had reported as of the end of September. Sanford also noted that NAR’s expenses as of late September had come in roughly $7 million better than budgeted, but that he expected some of those savings to be diminished by fourth quarter advocacy spending due to the recent midterm elections. Despite this, Sanford said that NAR’s cash and investments remain strong, allowing the trade group to meet its upcoming settlement payments while still investing in new products and services for its members. “In my two years as treasurer, I have seen the start of one of the greatest financial modernization in transformation in NAR's history,” Sanford said. “We have implemented a new accounting system along with accounting and budgeting tools, moved to monthly accrual accounting, selected and onboarded the new auditor, managed through massive personnel changes, implemented zero-based budgeting and now we are minutes away from voting to send our third consecutive balanced budget to the Board for approval.” Despite this progress, Sanford said that the work is not done, instead it's just getting started. 2027 Budget votes The next stage of this work kicked off with the approval of three budgetary members by the board of directors. Sanford noted that this budget was created after stringent review of each department, resulting in a budget “that is more intentional, more strategically aligned and better positioned to support [NAR’s] core mission while maintaining financial discipline.” During the meeting, the board overwhelmingly approved a 2027 operating and advocacy budget of $280,169,801 in gross revenue, and $246,952,390 in gross expenses. Over 90% of the directors also approved a 2027 consumer advertising campaign budget of $12 million in gross revenue and $13.696 million in program expenses. Additionally, over 95% of the directors approved a recommendation that found that the capital expenditure needs identified for 2027 technology total $2.42 million and that the capital expenditure needs identified for 2027 building needs total $3.06 million. Other measures approved In addition to approving budgetary measures, the board also voted on proposed amendments to the bylaws of the institutes, societies and councils. During the meeting, Brown noted that the amendments were reviewed by NAR’s general counsel and were deemed to be “not inconsistent with the policies and constitution” of NAR. The proposed amendments were approved by 864 directors voting in favor and six opposed. Beyond voting on these measures, the meeting also saw the installation of the 2027 leadership team, including 2027 NAR President Christine Hansen, a HousingWire Woman of Influence , President-elect Colin Mullane , First Vice President Pete Kopf and Treasurer Patti Fitzgerald. The leaders were approved by the board of directors back in May at NAR’s Realtors Legislative Meetings. Related More: Commission Lawsuit National Association of Realtors

items.title: Ryan Serhant’s firm aligns with American Real Estate Association to raise agent standards
items.description: SERHANT. , has joined the American Real Estate Association (ARA), adding a nationally recognized brand and sizable agent network to the trade group’s push to elevate professional standards and industry advocacy. The American Real Estate Association announced the move on Nov. 9, saying the addition of RealTrends Verified brokerage SERHANT. strengthens its national platform at a time when agent professionalism, consumer transparency and industry governance are under heightened scrutiny. Founded in 2020, SERHANT. describes itself as an AI-native real estate technology and media company with more than 2,000 agents across 20 states and Washington, D.C. The firm expanded beyond New York in 2023 and has since launched operations in California, Texas, Colorado, Massachusetts and Illinois in 2026, according to the company announcement. ARA positions itself as a national trade association “built for real estate agents, by real estate agents,” focused on advocacy, public education and higher professional standards. The organization said SERHANT. has been consistently ranked by RealTrends among the top private independent brokerages in the U.S. by sales volume, bringing additional production scale and media reach into the association. Co-founders Jason Haber and Mauricio Umansky framed the partnership as a step toward building a more unified industry voice. “When we launched ARA, our mission was clear: build a unified voice of reason, an association by agents, for agents, that relentlessly fights for the industry,” Haber and Umansky said in a joint statement. “Attaching Ryan Serhant and SERHANT. into this mission is a major step forward. It shows that this industry belongs to true professionals who are fiercely dedicated to their clients and to delivering the highest level of service.” Ryan Serhant, a broker, author and star and executive producer of Netflix’s “Owning Manhattan,” said the alignment is intended to give agents more leverage in today’s competitive, policy-driven housing market. “If you want to succeed in real estate today, you have to innovate, elevate and deliver unmatched value,” Serhant, founder and CEO of SERHANT., said. “ARA is doing the hard work to raise the bar for the entire profession while fighting for homeownership across the country. Aligning SERHANT. with ARA gives our agents an even stronger platform to educate consumers, advocate for clients and shape where this industry goes next.” SERHANT. joins REMAX , Compass International Holdings and Douglas Elliman among the larger brokerage networks that have aligned with ARA, according to the announcement. This year, ARA expanded its board with Chris Lim, former president and chief growth officer of REMAX , and investor Andrew Dodge. They serve alongside Douglas Elliman president and CEO Michael Liebowitz, Douglas Elliman general counsel Deva Roberts and Briggs Elwell. ARA has also been active on state policy issues with potential national implications. The association said it opposed Missouri’s Amendments 4 and 5 alongside the Missouri Association of Realtors. The ballot measures, which Missouri voters rejected in August, could have opened the door to transfer taxes on home sales and new taxes on real estate services. Why it matters for housing professionals The alignment gives ARA another large, media-savvy brokerage to amplify its advocacy work as litigation, regulatory shifts and local tax proposals reshape how agents operate and get paid. For brokers and team leaders, the move is another signal that major firms are investing in trade association strategies outside of traditional groups to influence policy, professional standards and consumer perception. items.title: Protesters Break Into Amsterdam Microsoft Data Center Site As Opposition Swells Across Europe
items.description: Around 150 to 200 protesters were arrested in Amsterdam last Friday after breaking into the construction site of a new Microsoft data center in an attempt to halt construction. Organized by the group Geef Tegengas, with participants from the grassroots organization Extinction Rebellion and pro-Palestine groups, it was the latest in a series of protests amid widespread backlash against data centers across Europe. Smaller protests took place the same day outside of a data center near Berlin, in Warsaw by the Polish parliament, at the main square in Zagreb, Croatia, in the center of Dublin, and in Bristol in the UK. Unsplash/Winston Chen The protests follow hot on the heels of U.S. midterm elections in which voters backed anti-data-center candidates at almost every level of government . Approximately 500 protesters broke into the Amsterdam site on Friday afternoon by breaking open the fence, while hundreds more gathered outside. Some demonstrators climbed onto cranes and the roof of the construction site near Sloterdijk train station in the Westpoort district. Another demonstration, organized by Fossiel Vrij Nederland in solidarity with the other groups, took place outside of the construction site, with 300 to 400 demonstrators joining in. “All over the world, ordinary people are resisting the construction of data centers. And rightly so: data centers guzzle water and energy, cause noise pollution, and contribute to the further heating of the planet,” Martijn Dekkers, spokesperson for Extinction Rebellion, said in a statement ahead of the protest. Police responded swiftly to protesters who broke into the site, arresting between 150 and 200 demonstrators who did not leave after being ordered to do so. Local news reports indicated that police used pepper spray and, in some cases, physical force to remove protesters who repeatedly ignored police requests. A spokesperson for Geef Tegengas, which translates to "give pushback," told local news broadcaster AT5 that they were displeased with the overall police response. “There is a right to demonstrate in this country, yet that right is being disregarded; even the march toward the data center was not facilitated,” a spokesperson said. A formal complaint was filed by the owner of the property, Oaktree-backed Pure Data Centres . “We understand that this project stirs up strong emotions, and we respect people’s right to express their opinions in a peaceful manner. However, we do not condone any actions that violate the law or put people’s safety at risk,” a Microsoft spokesperson said in a statement. The Microsoft data center in question, set to be the largest in Amsterdam, has been the subject of debate over the past few months. The facility consists of three 85-meter-tall towers, a design that bypasses current regulations for “hyperscale” data centers. Plans for the data center date back to 2016, before the municipality placed a ban on new data centers in the summer of 2019 due to grid capacity and land scarcity. The facility has changed hands twice since then. The facility does not fall under the national ban, in effect since Jan. 1, 2024, against large-scale data centers with a connection capacity of 70 megawatts or more and that span more than 10 hectares outside of the Eemshaven and Wieringermeer regions. The province of Noord-Holland previously stated that the plans predate the ban, and while the facility’s 78 MW capacity is above the limit, its built floor area is under 10 hectares. The protest comes as grid operators across the Netherlands struggle with congestion. Data centers are predicted to account for approximately 15% of the country's electricity use by 2030, up from 4.6% in 2024, according to Statistics Netherlands. items.title: Anthropic Pays $3.4B For Gas Turbines To Power Its Data Centers
items.description: Anthropic cut a $3.4B deal to speed up its access to power by purchasing its own gas turbines. Unsplash/American Public Power Association The artificial intelligence giant bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts worth of heavy-duty generators from San Antonio-based OnePWR Solutions, the Financial Times reported Sunday. The deal is the largest single purchase of equipment for power generation by an AI lab to date, according to the FT, and it comes as the race to build out data centers is increasingly constrained by access to energy. Anthropic, which is exploring a highly anticipated initial public offering as soon as this month, is taking over the generator contracts from Caterpillar , which initially ordered them from OnePWR two years ago but needed financing to complete the deal, the FT reported. Anthropic was already slated to become a customer of OnePWR, which sources turnkey behind-the-meter solutions for customers, before identifying the Caterpillar opportunity that includes the engineering and construction capabilities needed to install the generators. The power is expected to be available in the near term and over the next two years. OnePWR and Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Monday morning. Anthropic has disclosed nearly $900B in computing commitments through 2045. The artificial intelligence giant, best known for its Claude tool, made the first filings to disclose its plans to go public on Oct. 26 , setting the table for an IPO that will gauge investors’ appetite for massive valuations for the cash-burning frontier AI model firms. Anthropic’s IPO is expected to value the company at $1.5T, but major investors are skeptical that the AI giant can reach those heights, with one telling The Wall Street Journal the value could come in closer to $1T. Tech stocks with exposure to AI have been volatile this month, with a steep sell-off pushing the Nasdaq composite into correction territory on Thursday before recovering some of those losses Friday. The index continued to recover Monday, gaining more than 2% in premarket trading, but it is still down roughly 8% over the last month. The Anthropic IPO is being closely watched after rival OpenAI , the maker of ChatGPT, delayed plans to go public until next year and is instead trying to raise $20B at a $1.25T valuation, Bloomberg reported . Access to energy has long been a limiting factor in data center development that became more pressing after the 2022 launch of ChatGPT kicked off insatiable demand for computing power. The world’s biggest data center operators have set aggressive targets for cutting emissions on their expansive portfolios, but the rise of self-operated energy solutions and the need for fast access to power have made gas solutions increasingly popular. items.title: The Latest Shift in How Appraisals Are Handled Could Save Homebuyers Hundreds in Closing Costs—Eventually
items.description: It’s typically the last hurdle for homebuyers—and the process is about to get a face-lift. Last week, the Uniform Appraisal Dataset (UAD) 3.6 , a major update to property valuation standards introduced by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac , became mandatory for all new UCDP appraisal report submissions. UAD 3.6 is a new, digital form that appraisers will use to evaluate homes . Now, rather than the appraiser meticulously jotting down notes in longform paragraphs, the new system will allow appraisers to use extensive drop-down menus and checkboxes to make their evaluations. A proper appraisal can determine not only whether a buyer can qualify for a loan , but also whether they can save significant money at closing. Understanding the Uniform Appraisal Dataset 3.6 After a buyer makes an offer, their mortgage lender will order an independent appraisal to confirm the home is worth at least what's being borrowed against it. If the appraised value comes in at or above the purchase price, the process moves forward as planned. But if it comes in low, that gap has to be resolved before the loan can close. The logic behind the UAD 3.6 update, according to Fannie and Freddie, is to create a “data-driven, dynamic reporting structure to capture property and market information.” This new form includes significantly more data fields, helping lenders and buyers better understand the property’s characteristics. But with more detail comes a longer commitment. “Be prepared for a lot more questions from the appraiser during the inspection,” explains Michael Mignogna , president of the Appraisal Institute . “There’s a lot more data to include, so be prepared to answer questions about renovations, repairs, new systems like heating and air conditioning, appliances, etc., or have that information ready if no one with that type of information can be at the inspection.” To that end, with UAD 3.6, appraisers will now not only grade individual rooms, but they can also highlight upgrades and features that might’ve been lost in the old system. So, features of a newly remodeled kitchen or new bathroom flooring get specifically noted, which will aid in the ease of deciding the home’s value. Still, Mignogna is skeptical that this will have much of an impact on the final value. “Not as much information is always known about the comparables, so expectations about condition/quality adjustments to the comps on a room-by-room basis should be tempered,” he adds. Loading... Appraisers are different from inspectors, as they establish the home's value, not it's condition. Getty Images How these new appraisals can save buyers money The buyer almost always pays for the appraisal. The cost is typically a few hundred dollars, and it’s often rolled into closing costs. This is the case even though the appraiser is hired by the lender, not the buyer. The hope is that because this new appraisal process is a clean, digital checklist, banks can review and approve it much faster, reducing delays. For example, under the former process, lenders had the option to kick back the report for corrections if anything about the report was unclear, which could happen if the appraiser’s report didn’t cover every facet necessary. When that happens, buyers may find themselves having to pay for expensive mortgage rate-lock extensions to keep their rates while they wait for the appraisal to clear. Extension fees typically range from 0.125% to 0.250% (or up to 0.500% or more) of the buyer's total loan balance per extension period, often broken into 15-day increments. On a $450,000 mortgage, a 15-day extension would usually cost between $500 and $1,000. Given that closing costs already run a buyer anywhere from 2% to 5% of the total loan amount, or about $8,000 to $20,000 for a $400,000 loan, according to Bankrate , another couple hundred to a thousand dollars is nothing to scoff at. The flip side But as the saying goes, all good things come with time, and right now, this new digital infrastructure may actually be coming at a cost to buyers as it finds its footing. Clear Capital, a real estate valuation technology company, reported via National Mortgage Professional an average $65 increase in appraisal fees in markets where it has enough production volume to compare UAD 3.6 with the older UAD 2.6 format. Additionally, Michael Farrell , president of the National Association of Mortgage Brokers, said that the number of field appraisers equipped to do UAD 3.6 is so limited at this point, demand bottlenecks are driving up prices for modernized reports. While older appraisals are being priced at around $550, modernized reports may cost borrowers closer to $850. “It’s basically all roads lead to chaos,” Farrell explained to Scotsman Guide . “From an originator standpoint, it's a delay. Delays cost money. Delays cost the consumer money.” Mignogna, meanwhile, says it’s important to remember that fees are affected by far more than just the process. “Appraisal fees are very specific to markets and are affected by the number of appraisers in a market, the demand for appraisals in that market, interest rates, and a host of other factors,” he says. Having said that, the transition to the UAD 3.6 format continues to be slow and Mignogna concedes that lenders may bid up prices for the few field appraisers who are fully onboarded like in any “supply-demand situation.” But while delays are happening as appraisers go through a “transition mode,” Mignogna says this won’t affect buyers' need for expensive mortgage rate-lock extensions. “This is really only meaningful or significant in times of interest rate uncertainty or expected rate increases,” he says. “The overall UAD 3.6 process is longer right now for the reasons above, but as the learning curve flattens, turnaround times will improve. Chicago & Midwest + Midwest + Apartments | November 9, 2026 By: Jasmine Kilman CBRE Arranges $30M Sale of Multifamily Portfolio in Madison CBRE has arranged the sale of a two-property multifamily portfolio totaling 108 units in Madison. Back Nine Acquisitions, LLC, purchased the property from Flad Development & Investments for $29.95 million. CBRE’s Gretchen Richards, Matson Holbrook and Sean Beuche represented the seller in the transaction. The portfolio includes The Tradition at Smoky’s Club, a 59-unit property located at 3007 University Ave., and The Whitney Reserve, a 49-unit property located at 5201 Old Middleton Road. Together, the properties include over 2,400 square feet of ground-floor retail space in Madison’s West submarket. “Demand for high-quality multifamily properties in Madison remains strong, specifically for newly constructed properties in prime locations,” said Richards. “This portfolio drew in significant interest from both local and national investors due to the choice locale, discerning design decisions, and attentive management.” The properties are located 1.4 miles apart, each situated near Madison’s Hilldale Shopping Center and offering convenient access to downtown Madison, the University of Wisconsin–Madison, and UW Health. items.title: MacKenzie Brokers $11M Sale of 106K-SF Warehouse in MD
items.description: MacKenzie Brokers $11M Sale of 106K-SF Warehouse in MD VeryBest Wholesales, a general merchandise distribution and digital ordering platform, has acquired 4665 Hollins Ferry Road, a single-story warehouse building comprising 105,732 square feet of space for $11.45 million from Saver Automotive Products. MacKenzie Commercial Real Estate Services Senior Vice President and Principal Matthew Curran, SIOR and Andrew Meeder brokered the transaction. VeryBest Wholesales is relocating its distribution operation from 8263 Patuxent Range Road in Jessup to Halethorpe in Baltimore County. Delivered in 1972 and situated on an approximately five-acre site adjacent to Interstate 895, the building features 24-foot ceiling heights, eleven loading docks, one drive-in door, and 9,345 square feet of office space on a mezzanine level. The site is situated less than one mile from Interstate 695, two miles from Interstate 95 and MD Route 295, and six miles from the Fairfield Marine Terminal. items.title: Larkspur Capital Begins Leasing 219-Unit Multifamily Project in Dallas
items.description: Larkspur Capital Begins Leasing 219-Unit Multifamily Project in Dallas by Taylor Williams November 9, 2026 November 9, 2026 4 DALLAS — Locally based developer Larkspur Capital has begun leasing The Juniper , a 219-unit multifamily project in Dallas. The site is located within a Qualified Opportunity Zone at 4003 Commerce St. in the Exposition Park area of Dallas. The site spans 1.4 acres, and the property feature studio, one- and two-bedroom units in addition to townhomes, penthouses and ground-floor retail space. Amenities include a pool, dog park, fitness center, multiple lounges, pickleball courts, outdoor grilling and dining stations and a clubhouse. Corgan designed the project, with Faulkner Design Group handling interior architecture. OHT Partners served as the general contractor. Rents start at roughly $1,600 per month for a studio apartment. items.title: The ‘Blue Wave’ Swept Top Homebuilding States. What Happens Next?
items.description: On Tuesday, the governor’s offices in five states were swept up by the “blue wave,” as Democrats were elected to succeed current Republican leadership. Iowa , Georgia , Nevada , Ohio , and Texas all flipped the governor’s seat from Republican to Democrat, after Democrats campaigned heavily on issues of affordability. Of those five states, four rank in the top 15 on the Realtor.com® state Affordability & Homebuilding Report Cards for 2026, after making strides to expand housing supply under GOP leadership. The report cards rank states on a points scale based on two major factors: affordability, such as the share of the state’s median income required to afford its median-priced home, and homebuilding, whether states are producing enough new housing to keep up with demand. With affordability sticking out among the most important voter issues this year, how the new Democratic administrations improve, or at least maintain, states’ housing markets will be vital to whether they’re deemed successful. Loading... Iowa Democrat Rob Sand was selected by the voters of Iowa in an 11-point victory over Republican Zach Lahn . He will take over the position from outgoing Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds . Iowa was ranked second in the 2026 state report cards, earning a total score of 75.8 out of 100 for a grade of A. However, Iowa’s strength lies in the affordability aspect of the grading scale, not homebuilding. The state’s median listing price sits at $282,886, which calls for just 25.4% of the $75,991 median income, giving it a Realtor Affordability Score of 0.96. The downside comes in its homebuilding numbers. Iowa accounts for just 0.94% of the country’s issued building permits. While that number is on par with population—Iowa accounts for a 0.95% share of the country’s population—the state’s 56% new-construction premium indicates that builders are focused on larger, more expensive homes, rather than entry-level inventory and affordable builds. In his “Truer Better Agenda,” Sand acknowledged that Iowa needs to build 21,000 more homes by 2030 to address the state’s housing shortage and improve affordability. Within his platform, he states his intention to work with the Legislature to ensure more homes, and more types of homes, are built. “We need to cut the bureaucratic red tape that often stands in the way of that by simplifying the permitting and inspections process to reduce administrative time, redundant inspections, and costs for Iowa families,” reads Sand’s agenda. Beyond building, Sand’s platform includes protecting renters from price gouging and removing interest from Iowa’s down payment and homebuyer assistance programs. Jay Iverson , executive officer at the Home Builders Association of Iowa, said they have already been meeting with Sand to work on improving the regulatory process in the state, but the newly elected governor will face his share of challenges. “He’ll still have a Republican-led House and Senate, so they’re going to have to figure out a way to get along. We fight the regulatory issues all the time, code updates, and all of the things that add significant costs,” Iverson told Realtor.com. “So we’re meeting with him even currently, before he’s sworn in, and hoping to deliver on that message of regulatory relief.” Iverson said he’s looking forward to seeing Sand’s administration work with other governmental bodies to make improvements for Iowans, especially as the two parties come together. “It’s just going to be a different environment. He sold himself during the campaign on, 'We should all be able to get along, let’s figure this out,’ and I think we’re going to hold him to that,” said Iverson. “I’m looking forward to that part, just seeing what actually happens and how it works. It’s never easy.” Texas Texas saw a major upset on Tuesday, when the state elected a Democratic governor for the first time since 1991. Gina Hinojosa , who will make history as Texas’ first Latina elected governor, denied incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott a fourth term with her 7-point victory. Texas is a consistent front-runner in the Realtor.com state report cards, coming in at No. 4 in 2026. The Lone Star State received a score of 71 out of 100 for a grade of A-. Its success in the rankings is due to Texas being the nation’s largest homebuilder, accounting for 14.6% of all building permits issued in the country. This far outpaces any other state and is well above the state’s 9.3% population share. The new-construction premium in Texas is only 7.6%, indicating that builders are adding affordable and competitively priced homes to the state’s inventory. However, the state struggles slightly with affordability, with the median listing price of $364,749 taking up 32.5% of the state’s median income, giving it a Realtor Affordability Score of 0.66. Housing has long been a priority of Hinojosa, who has been fighting against multinational corporations and predatory landlords since she was elected to the Texas House of Representatives in 2017. In 2025, she authored a bill that would prevent institutional investors from snapping up more than 10 single-family homes. As governor, she intends to keep fighting corporate investors and price gouging that keep affordable housing and homeownership out of reach of Texans, according to her campaign . Loading... items.title: What NAR's new MLS policy options mean for data feeds and licensing
items.description: The National Association of Realtors (NAR) has approved four multiple listing service (MLS) policy recommendations that increase MLSs’ options to claim copyright in listing content, expand local flexibility on data feeds, clarify permissible uses of MLS data and update qualifications for NAR’s MLS Committee. The recommendations from NAR’s Multiple Listing Issues and Policies Committee were considered and adopted at NAR NXT 2026 conference on Sunday and are tied to the trade group’s 2026-2028 strategic plan to modernize MLS policies, the association said in an announcement Sunday. New optional copyright policy for MLS data The most consequential change for brokers and MLS operators is a revision to MLS Policy Statement 7.85 and the creation of a new optional policy on copyright protection of MLS data. Under the revised policy, MLSs may, at their discretion, require up to a 50% copyright interest in certain listing content to strengthen copyright enforcement, subject to quarterly copyright registration requirements. MLSs must give participants the right to opt out of assigning a copyright interest to the MLS, and brokers retain the right to independently use and license their own listing content. Copyright ownership and enforcement have become more important as listing photos and data are syndicated across portals, IDX sites and marketing platforms, and as MLSs face more frequent questions and disputes about unauthorized scraping and reuse of listing content. Greater local flexibility on data feeds NAR also adopted an optional MLS policy on MLS data feed services. The policy allows MLSs to establish local eligibility and licensing requirements for data feeds, as long as those rules are reasonable, objective and applied equally to all participants. Even with new local rules, participants must retain access to MLS listing information and data feeds for their own listings. For brokers and vendors, this could affect how quickly and under what conditions they can obtain broader data feeds for tools such as brokerage websites, back-office systems and analytics products, depending on how individual MLSs choose to implement the optional policy. Clarification on permitted MLS data uses A new MLS policy statement reinforces that the use of MLS data must comply with applicable MLS participation or data licensing agreements and must be connected to real estate brokerage services, the preparation of appraisals or other valuations of real property. NAR said this is intended to address concerns around unauthorized use of MLS content, including use cases that are not connected to providing brokerage or valuation services. For MLSs, this language provides additional backing for enforcement actions against parties that use listing data for unrelated commercial purposes. For brokers and appraisers, it underscores the need to align technology partnerships and data workflows with the scope of their MLS agreements. Updated qualifications for NAR’s MLS Committee NAR also updated the qualification criteria for service on its MLS Committee. The changes are meant to better reflect today’s MLS environment and ensure the committee includes members with relevant industry expertise and perspectives. While specific qualification details were not outlined in the announcement, changes to committee composition can influence how future policy recommendations are shaped and how regional and business-model interests are represented at the national level. “These updates reflect our commitment to ensuring MLS policies remain relevant, effective, and responsive to the needs of today’s real estate industry,” Nykia Wright, the CEO of NAR and a 2026 HousingWire Woman of Influence and Vanguard award winner, said in the announcement. “In line with our 2026–2028 Strategic Plan and significant member feedback, we will continue working collaboratively with MLSs, brokers, members, and other industry partners to support a clear understanding and implementation of these changes.” Next steps for MLSs and brokers Because several of the policies are optional , local MLSs will have to decide whether and how to adopt them. MLS executives and boards will likely review their copyright strategies, data feed agreements and committee engagement structures in light of the new framework. Brokers, teams and technology vendors should review their MLS participation and data licensing agreements to understand how any local policy changes could affect website data feeds, marketing uses of listing content and third-party integrations.
